speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, October 29, consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-80, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be allowed to join in the debate on Bill C-80 this morning. There are several points that I would like to make over the next 10 minutes. I would like to refresh the memory of the House regarding some of the campaign promises made one year ago and relate them to Bill C-80.
It was only 14 months ago, in the midst of a national election campaign, that a promise was made by Conservative Members that if they were to take office, any budgetary measures they would introduce would ensure that more resources would be placed in the hands of those who need them the most. That was going to be the guiding principle of the Government. Since that time, all Canadians have had time to digest the over-all direction of the Government. Upon reflection, I think most of us would have to agree that if anything, once again the Conservative Government has broken its promise to put more into the hands of those who need it the most. Bill C-80 is a good example of that.
As was pointed out at a press conference held some 10 or 12 days ago by the National Anti-Poverty Organization, Bill C-80, an Act to increase excise and federal sales taxes, will impact twice as hard on the poor as it will on upper-income earners. In an analysis of the impact of this budgetary measure, the organization points out that excise taxes and sales taxes are regressive because of that. As a result, the organization would like the Government to withdraw the Bill and bring in one that is progressive to some degree.
It comes as no surprise to the Opposition that the Government has again introduced a Bill that is regressive in nature. One need look no further back than to the impact of the deindexation of personal exemptions in the May 23 Budget. I have pointed out time and again that that measure alone will
do more to widen the gap between the poor and the rich than any other budgetary measure that the Government could possibly bring in. Yet my complaints seem to have fallen upon deaf ears. All Conservative back-benchers represent constituents but they have been amazingly silent on this issue. It comes as no surprise to the Opposition that they would be silent on the matter. However, it is incumbent upon the Opposition to point out the folly of the Government's direction.
I said earlier that Bill C-80, the Bill to increase the excise and federal sales taxes, is regressive in nature. 1 would indicate as well that the deindexation of personal exemptions will be even more so. What is the full import of that kind of change in policy direction by the Government? It is astounding.
The various social council agencies that give advice to the Government including the Canadian Council on Social Development and the National Council on Welfare have had things to say about this impact. In a study released just two months ago, they indicated that from 1980 to 1984, before the Conservative Government came to power, there had been a widening in the gap between the poor and the rich. Despite all of the Guaranteed Income Supplement measures that the previous Government introduced between 1980 and 1984, the gap was still widening largely as a result of the recession. Clearly the point I am making is that there was a widening in the gap between the poor and the rich in those four years. Now, on top of all the other problems that are besetting the lower-income groups in our society, deliberate Government policy is going to widen that gap further.
The councils to which I refer have made some calculations and these numbers are not disputed by the Government, by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) or by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). They indicate that because of the deindexation of personal exemptions, a family that earns $15,000 per year is going to pay an additional $1,879 in taxes over the next five years. A family that earns $35,000 per year, a middle-income family, is going to pay an additional $3,450 in income tax over the next five years. However, what happens to the family that earns $80,000 per year? Amazingly, it will only have to pay an additional $1,612 in taxes over the next five years. In other words, the councils that represent middle and lower-income earners question the political and social policy direction of the Government, a direction that will widen that gap despite the fact that they have clearly shown that as a result of the recession, lower-income Canadians are the ones who have suffered the most in the last four years. They are now expected to suffer doubly over the next four to five years as a result of the Government's proposals.

Excise Tax Act
I indicated to the House that the report of the National Anti-Poverty Organization indicated that the impact of the federal excise tax will be twice as hard on the poor in our society. More important, the organization indicated something which I think should clearly be at the heart of the debate, not only with respect to the excise and federal sales tax measures but with respect to the direction of the May 23 Budget. The organization shows that the most important source of revenue for the federal Government comes from taxes, which comes as no surprise. Everyone knows that if we have expenditures and Government programs someone has to pay for them. Amazingly, of the S63.8 billion derived from tax revenue in 1984-85, fully 90 per cent of that came from personal income tax and from commodity taxes and the rest was derived from miscellaneous and corporate income tax.
Corporate income tax in the country in the last two and a half decades accounts for a decreasing share of tax revenue for Governments. Here we have a situation in which, once again, we will have to pay increased taxes under the May 23 Budget. If anything, these corporations have been given more tax breaks. Members who have spoken on these measures, and other Bills, have indicated our displeasure with respect to them. Corporations are not being asked to pay increased taxes. Rather, middle income and low income Canadians are being asked to pay more, which is why we are so disturbed that, seemingly, the Government does not understand why the social policy direction inherent in not only this Bill but in others is being opposed by the majority of Canadians. Yet, every time we raise the issue during Question Period the answer comes back to us in terms of: "What are you complaining about? The Government has certain measures which will, in fact, put more into the hands of the poor". Nothing could be further from the actual case.
I ask Hon. Members to consider Bill C-70, a Bill which proposes deindexation of family allowances. We have had the opportunity to review this Bill clause by clause with expert witnesses who have appeared before the committee. Every one of the social policy agencies in the country and every one of the groups which represent women and the poor in our society have indicated the falling off of the Government's social policy direction as a result of the May 23 Budget. I include in this category specific groups which do not represent national interests but pockets of poverty-stricken individuals in communities in Calgary, Saskatoon and so on.
This is why members of the Opposition are so adamant about ensuring that the Government bears in mind that the interests of our constituents, middle income and low income Canadians, are well served by our opposition to these types of Bills. I understand, of course, that with 211 Members, the Government can do exactly as it pleases. However, we want to ensure that the Government bears in mind the interests of our constituents when it introduces Bills such as C-70 and C-80 and, of course, other Bills which will be introduced with respect to changes in the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the House for this opportunity to speak to Bill C-80. Quite frankly, the responsible but painful decision we are about to make is merely the result of the policy the previous Government maintained for fifteen years without any regard for sound financial administration.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-80, the legislation before the House today that concerns federal sales and excise taxes, is aimed at reversing the considerable erosion of the federal tax base caused by a lack of leadership on the part of the previous Government, which spent money without worrying about where it would come from. Red stands for Liberals, and they were indeed in the red.
The question we must ask ourselves today is, again quite frankly: Why are we obliged to impose these tax increases?
Mr. Speaker, this Bill should be seen within the context of the changes and proposals announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) last May. This Bill is a financial measure, and its purpose is mainly to keep our national debt within bounds through a number of measures that either produce revenue or reduce tax expenditures.
Unfortunately, I will now have to remind my hon. friends opposite of some of the consequences of their actions, actions that caused them to lose power, and subsequently, Canadians inherited a cumulative debt unprecedented in our history.
In 1968, only seventeen years ago, Mr. Speaker, our country had a budgetary surplus of $750,000, and now, seventeen years later, the country's national debt has risen to $200 billion, while interest rates have reached unprecedented levels, and I am thinking here of people who have payments to make on their homes, and I remember two years ago when we had interest rates of up to 18 per cent and even more, bringing Canadian industry to the very brink of bankruptcy, and causing the country's gross national product to drop so dramatically that around 1982, people were wondering whether Canada, as a result of the policies of the Liberal Government at the time, had become a country where the slogan was no longer "back to the land" but "into the ground".
Mr. Speaker, whatever my friends opposite may think, 1 take no pleasure at all in reminding Canadians of a time we would all like to forget. Mr. Speaker, forget is the word, because that time is certainly not representative of the imagination, know-how and courage of the Canadian people. During that time we were misled and deceived by the outward appearance of a serious Government, by a marvelous exercise in camouflage, by a flood of promises. On September 4, 1984, people across Canada finally realized it was time to hand the reins of power to a more responsible party that would not be
November 5, 1985

afraid to bring this country's economy back to economic liberalism, and to focus on private enterprise and job creation.
The people were undeniably right, and in less than one year, our Government was able to restore the confidence of the people in their Government. However, Mr. Speaker, our Government did not mislead the people by telling them it would be easy. It did not claim, as some politicians do, often with a lot of political rhetoric, that all we need would be some legislation that would pay off in the next election. No, Mr. Speaker. By electing this Government, Canadians were putting common sense back into Government, and in doing so, they fully realized that they would have to do their share to help industry get back on its feet, a sector the previous Government preferred to ignore.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, Hon. Members opposite see confidence as an indispensable stimulus for democratic and capitalist societies, for societies that are creative and innovative. A man who is afraid of tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, is only happy in the security of the status quo, and he does not evolve. For fifteen years, Canadians have been kept in a state of non-confidence in the future, and they could no longer create or take risks or invent as they had before.
My colleagues in the Progressive Conservative Party and 1 are no longer interested in blaming the current situation on the previous Government, but in showing that one can achieve anything when one has both knowledge and confidence. We can go from a situation which is far from enviable to an environment which could be promising indeed.
Mr. Speaker, that is what we are doing now. Canadians have renewed confidence, as demontrated by various indicators. People are investing again, thereby creating hundreds of thousands of new jobs. Our trade unions, provincial Governments, and all economic agents generally are working together again, dialoguing and looking forward to rebuilding our country. Such are the indicators of the Canadian economy. It has been showing increasingly more evident signs of vigor ever since our coming to power. The number of jobs has increased, interest rates have come down, investors are showing signs of renewed confidence, consumer spending is rising, prices are stable and there are fewer and fewer bankruptcies. Moreover, the performance of our economy is superior to that of the United States.
Employmentwise, Mr. Speaker, we have created 304,000 new jobs over the past year. The unemployment figure, which was 11.6 per cent, is now down to 10.1 per cent. This is not yet excellent, but I suggest this shows a definite improvement and a very positive trend which should be emphasized.
Mr. Speaker, the era of arrogance and darkness has finally ended. We all know now that by working together, we will rebuild what others have demolished. We all know also that this will require the joint effort of all Canadians, but we are ready to pay the price for our own good and that of future generations of Canadians.
Excise Tax Act
In fact, when 1 adhered to this party and this Government, 1 was fully aware that I was getting involved with all other Canadians in a national effort to reestablish a climate of confidence.
Knowing full well that Canada absolutely needs to replenish its coffers, that it is back on the right track, and that we are about to shelve 15 years of poor performance, we must continue without sparing our efforts. Because of his trust in the support and good sense of the Canadian people, the Minister of Finance moved ahead in May and introduced a new budget. Three of every four measures in this budget were aimed at reducing expenditures. Bill C-80, which has now reached 2nd reading, will increase our revenues by $2.5 billion.
The purpose of this legislation, which should have been adopted a long time ago but which was not for some dark election-oriented reason, is to increase the sales tax base, leaving about 30 per cent of commodities which could be taxed on the federal level. This sales tax, as we all know, is one of the Government's main source of income. However, throughout the years a very long list of tax-free products has kept getting longer and longer, thus depriving the Government of Canada of massive revenues which would have allowed us to reduce the deficit and promote confidence. We are now proposing that those products be no longer tax-free.
Mr. Speaker, once again this Government having succeeded, thanks to its sincere and honest attitude, in dispelling strains and easing the situation in economic, social and political sectors; having succeeded in restoring confidence and thus lowering the unemployment rate; having succeeded in replacing workers' assistance and meaningless programs with programs stimulating effort and the will to learn; having succeeded in reducing interest rates which are a burden for millions of heads of families, because the previous Government had not found anything better to control inflation than raising interest rates, we are asking Canadians to let us carry on with what we have so well started and to give us the means to do it.
Before concluding my comments, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the 2nd Annual Report of the Economic Council of Canada on economic forecasts and this is what its chairman, Mr. David Slater stated: "Economic forecasts for Canada are gradually improving and indicate a stable growth in the medium term. The Gross National Product could increase by an average of 3.5 per cent during the next decade and the inflation rate would be around 4 per cent per year as of 1990 and would fall to a lower level during the following five years."
The Economic Council of Canada expects that unemployment will decrease gradually to an average of 9 per cent between 1985 and 1990 and to 7.6 per cent during the following five years. Our federal deficit will continue to decrease in proportion to our Gross National Product. I think

that it is quite an encouraging indication provided by the Economic Council of Canada.
We are now asking the Canadian people to support Bill C-80 now before this House in order to proceed with our economic revival and to reduce the deficit. It is not easy, Mr. Speaker, but we must do so if we want our economy to become healthier.

Mr. Speaker, I find it rather strange and somewhat disquieting to be debating Bill C-80, which introduces some very unfair tax measures which make no economic sense, and to be doing so under the guillotine. Closure has a purpose and validity in our Standing Orders, Mr. Speaker, as all Members of Parliament know, but I doubt very much whether it has validity when the Party in power has such a massive majority. I doubt whether the Canadian people would agree that a closure motion is justified when there is a huge majority on the government side and a small Opposition. Mind you, this small Opposition has proven to be very vigorous and very effective. If any Members have failed to comprehend that, they need only ask the senior citizens of the country how, when we combined forces with them, we were able to cause the Government to retreat from a mean and vindictive reduction of senior citizens' pensions.
However, I doubt whether closure has any validity on a tax grab Bill such as C-80. We all know that the sales tax is regressive. It hurts most those who can least afford to lose those extra precious dollars. It increases the Consumer Price Index. I suppose we have become lethargic about inflation, but it is still with us and it concerns most those who have the fewest dollars to spend. It is into the pockets of those people that we are reaching with these petty tax grabs which make no economic sense at all.
For example, we are going to add another tax on gasoline. In the region of the country from which I come, Mr. Speaker, gasoline is already too expensive. In fact, we pay the highest price for gasoline in the country apart from that paid in the far north. We pay much more than motorists pay elsewhere and it is hurting our tourist industry. I really wonder how the Members from northern Ontario who sit on the Government side could allow this additional tax on gasoline to be introduced through a Bill such as C-80. How do the Member for Timis-kaming (Mr. MacDougal!) and the Member for Timmins-Chapleau (Mr. Gervais) justify to their constituents a higher tax on gasoline?
I see that the Hon. Member for Timmins-Chapleau is present in the House today. He indicated recently that he wants to be my partner. He wants to work with me for a better deal for northern Ontario. He indicated that he has much greater access to Cabinet Ministers. I rejected his offer of a partnership, Mr. Speaker. I said: "Thanks, but no thanks". I want to confess that perhaps I was just a bit hasty. I would like to reconsider that offer. I would like the Member for Timmins-Chapleau to prove to me, to his constituents and to my
constituents that he can do something about this tax on gasoline. Can he get the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to roll back this increased tax on gasoline? If he can, perhaps I will reconsider his offer of a partnership. After all, I recognize that we are not here to serve our political Parties, but to serve our constituents. If we can get this tax rolled back, perhaps the Member for Timmins-Chapleau and myself can join forces and get a better deal for northern Ontario from the Government which has already done so much to downgrade this region with regard to job creation programs and regional development programs. So much has been done in such a short time to undo the good work of the previous Liberal administration in northern Ontario.
Let us talk for a moment about the increase in the price of gasoline. If one includes the increase in the general excise tax plus the higher gasoline price, it means that the price of gasoline will rise by approximately 4 per cent. According to the figures from the Tourism Industry Association, a 4 per cent fuel price increase translates into 900,000 fewer American visitors coming to Canada. The Member for Timmins-Chapleau knows that many of those visitors come to northern Ontario and that we want more of them.
On a typical day a visitor may spend about $82. The multiplier effect for every dollar is approximately $1.79. Therefore we can come to the conclusion that this increase in the price of gasoline will cost our economy, in tourism dollars, approximately $135 million. That is why I say it is an unfair tax that makes no economic sense. Furthermore, about 5,325 tourism jobs will be lost.
I do not know what happened in Cabinet when this issue came up but I must believe that the Minister of State for Tourism (Mr. Murta) must have fought like a mad dog against that increase. He must have dug in his heels to say to his colleagues in Cabinet: "No way will I allow that kind of an increase. It hurts my national constituency. I am fighting for the tourist industry in this country and will not let that happen". The Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) from Sault Ste. Marie must have been right there to give his support to the Minister of State for Tourism. When this issue came up in caucus I imagine the Member for Timiskaming and the Member for Timmins-Chapleau must have joined forces with those two Ministers to stop this tax increase, but to no avail.
We will feel the effects of this on the economy of northern Ontario because Members from northern Ontario will know that the forest industry has stabilized and is not creating any new jobs. Pulp prices are depressed. There is no expanding market so that we cannot look to forestry for new jobs. We are holding our own, but not growing.
Mining is in a depressed state, except for gold, so that we cannot look for any hope there unless international metal prices suddenly show a significant increase. We know that the market for metals is saturated so that we cannot look to that industry to produce jobs.
November 5, 1985

Tourism is the sector which can provide jobs and encourage the economy of a region like northern Ontario. However, the Government has slapped on an additional tax that will affect our tourist industry which is already having difficulty matching costs in the United States for such things as fuel, accommodation and liquor. This increase in tax will add to an already intolerable situation.
Bill C-80 is a series of unfair taxes that make no economic sense at all. Let me give another illustration. Canadians should be aware that, incredibly, Bill C-80 will tax alternative energy and energy conservation equipment. Let me cite some of those items which will be taxed at the 11 per cent level, beginning January 1 next year: heat recovery units and devices for extracting heat from exhaust air or waste water for recovery of energy; solar panels and tubes for collecting and converting solar energy; wood-burning stoves and space heaters. The following items will be taxed at 7 per cent construction rate: heat pumps in permanent heating systems; wrapping material and thermal insulation designed for pipes and ducts in buildings and mechanical systems; loading dock seals and shelters.
The measures being imposed in Bill C-80 will not result in any great tax revenue to the Government but will discourage Canadians from improving the efficiency with which they use energy.
Because Bill C-80 imposes unfair taxes and makes no economic sense, the Government, being very embarrassed about it, imposes time allocation. I have said that there is a proper moment, with certain Bills, to use time allocation. However, this is not one of those Bills.
Let us see how Bill C-80 will affect the construction industry. There are hundreds of small and medium sized construction companies which will see their profit margins cut to the bone. They will be forced to absorb a new 6 per cent tax on construction materials which will place them in difficulty because many of these contractors are on a fixed contract and cannot adjust their contracts to meet this new tax. Therefore, the profit margin is lost.
One modest and very practical suggestion was that the tax be phased in to take account of the fixed price contracts. However, the Government ignored that suggestion.
When this Budget measure is added to other Government measures such as higher fuel costs, CMHC cut-backs and the elimination of the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan, it will add up to a very heavy blow to the industry at a critical time when it was beginning to recover. That industry will be cut back as a result of these unfair taxes that make no economic sense at all.
Even the children will not be spared. There will be an unfair tax increase on chewing gum, candy and pet food. It makes no economic sense at all.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on this matter but having heard the
Excise Tax Act
presentation by the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), I cannot restrain myself from saying just a few words.
The Hon. Member is one who presents himself as a very reasonable person. In fact, he has a reputation for that and, in the past, it has been a well deserved reputation for reasonableness. However, he has thrown it all away today. 1 never heard such a blatant partisan argument as that presented by him today. There was not one iota of reason contained therein.
He argued that during the time of the Liberal Government it was acceptable to impose closure time and time again as a regular means of operation because there were more Members in the opposition. He went on to state that today that process, which is permitted in the Standing Orders of the House, should not be used because there are slightly fewer Members in the Opposition. That makes no sense because it is a well known fact that a small number of Members in the Opposition, by introducing amendment after amendment and recycling speakers, can tie up House business on a filibuster just as well as if there were another 30 or 40 Members. There is no difference when there is an opportunity to recycle speakers.
Unfortunately, the tactics that have been used by the present Opposition are precisely that. Their sole strategy appears to be to tie up the work of Parliament because they have no alternative policies to put forward. They have no real logical arguments to make that would propose better legislation. They are simply tying up Parliament and doing the Canadian people no benefit whatsoever by that type of tactic. They are forcing the Government to use these provisions in the Standing Orders.
I would agree to a certain extent with the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior that this is not the right way of proceeding. I understand that other Parliaments throughout the Commonwealth have developed a better system. Why is it not possible for us to use existing Standing Orders to allow the various Parties to decide how to deal with a measure such as Bill C-80? Everyone knows that it will be passed into law at some point because it is necessary legislation. This Bill is worth four or five days of debate and the Parties could sit down to organize such a debate and come to an agreement so that we do not have to use the time allocation system constantly. We certainly need a better system than that.
The Bill before us provides a means of raising the revenue for expenses that the Government will incur. These expenses include the old age pension. This again was referred to in the speech of the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior. He was condemning this legislation and at the same time praising his own Party's position concerning the old age pension.
If we are to have indexed old age pensions, it will cost hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars. The Government cannot give something it does not first take away from somebody else. You cannot argue, on the one hand, for higher old age pensions, Mr. Speaker, and then, when the tax bill comes in to pay for it, say: "No, no, we should not raise that additional revenue". Anybody of a sound mind has to realize

November 5, 1985
Excise Tax Act
that if you want something, you have to pay for it. You cannot be like a child and say: "We want this and this". One cannot say, "We want more and more," as the Opposition says, and then when the time comes to pay say, "No, we are not prepared to pay for it."
If the public is to have any confidence in Parliament and any confidence in the Opposition-and what little bit the Opposition has in gradually slipping away-one has to take that sensible, reasonable and logical position and know one has to pay for anything given away by Government.
Regarding the sales tax, it is very easy to score political points by saying that any particular item should be exempt from sales tax, such as children's candy, for example. Who wants to put a tax on children's candy? Let us select another item, medical supplies, for instance. One hears: "We don't want to put a tax on that". You can come up with an argument on just about any single item as to why should not be taxed. It does not matter whether it is a cup of coffee, a cubic yard of cement, or whatever. You can always think of good arguments to exclude a specific item. If we allow ourselves to be persuaded by those who would argue that there should not be a tax levied on a particular item, one would find that the sales tax base would decrease, and on those items still taxed, the taxes would be horrendous in order to raise necessary moneys for other things.
What this Government has been trying to do is to be fair and say that everything, as much as possible, should be included in the tax base, so as to have as low an over-all rate as possible. Not only that, you have much less administration if you do not have special rates for special items or exclusions. Sometimes you exclude one thing that is substituted by something else, which creates a terrible administrative problem as the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) can well describe.
As a final point, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a good thing about the Bill in that it extends the right of appeal and the right not to pay taxes until-if you want to dispute the tax levied-the matter has been decided by a court of law. Another good thing is to extend the provisions which were recently incorporated with respect to income taxes-those provisions which were included in the Progressive Conservative taxpayers' bill of rights-to excise and sales tax matters. That is certainly a step in the right direction.
Thank you for the opportunity, Sir, to refute some of the remarks made by my good friend and colleague from Cochrane-Superior.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when speaking on this legislation with the threat of time allocation hanging over our heads, it is important to remember that time allocation is getting to be a consistent policy of the Government. The Conservative Party, now in Government, used to oppose time allocation when it was in opposition. Yet we are in the ironical situation that on almost every piece of legislation coming to the House at present the Government is preventing full debate.

speechtext:
One of my colleagues calls it shameful. I am not allowed to say that it is hypocritical because that is not allowed by the rules of the House, but it is something close to hypocritical when you do one thing in opposition and the exact opposite when in government.
Tax policy is one of the very areas on which the House of Commons should be spending a fair amount of time. It is evident from the Auditor General's Report that we, as the watchdogs of the Government purse and as the people who are passing legislation resulting in tax increases, are not doing a very effective job. Much of that is because we are not getting the information we need from the Government, whether the present Conservative Government or the previous Liberal Government. In addition, the whole structure in a lot of these debates does not allow for the real investigation necessary, something we will have to look at in terms of Parliament itself.
By bringing in time allocation on this Bill and forcing it through the House later today, the Government is preventing us from moving in the direction which the Auditor General called for in his report last week.
We are also rushing this piece of legislation through which will increase taxes, hidden taxes for the most part, on Canadians without any real study of alternatives and without any real attempt by the Government to look at tax reform.
There is no introduction of a minimum tax for the rich. There is no change in the corporation tax. There is no concept of fairer taxation. What we have is a minor series of amendments which will add to the tax bill of ordinary Canadians. As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) pointed out, in some cases that will especially hurt people from northern regions because higher gas, oil and aviation taxes increase the cost of living in those regions. Yet here we are rushing a Bill through the House with no consideration as to how it will affect people in northern Ontario, the Northwest Territories or northern Manitoba.
In September, 1984, Canadians did vote for a change. They wanted to see their Government open things up. Canadians wanted to see some type of fair taxation system introduced. Yet much of this legislation before us today has been introduced by previous Liberal Governments. It is the same system. All we see is percentages increased by 1 per cent here or 2 per cent there to increase the revenue to the federal Government.
I object to the quick passage of this Bill without any chance for public input, without any chance for a study as to how taxes should be raised and where the money should come from. At the same time, the Government is constantly spending. We have seen a billion dollars go in tax write-offs for the Gulf deal, another billion dollars went into the tax write-off in the Dome deal, and we have seen another piece of legislation rushed through the House for a billion dollar bank bail-out. The Government is spending billions upon billions on tax write-offs and in bank bail-out money, yet it says it needs to increase the money collected from ordinary Canadians.
If you have these bail-outs and give money away or refuse to take money owing to the Government of Canada on various oil
November 5, 1985

company deals, and if you are to give something like $9 billion to the oil industry as a result of the May 23 Budget, you will have to increase taxes and take away money from the taxpayers, people who will not benefit from the billion dollar bail-outs.
Worse than that, Mr. Speaker, some of the other things the Government is doing indicate there is no sense of fair taxation. The Conservative Government is to continue along the same trail which Liberal Governments followed in the past.
Let met quote from a speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to the Canadian Tax Foundation in November, 1984 when he said:
Our recent figures indicate that the effect of tax incentives has been to reduce the average federal corporate income tax rate from 36 per cent to 15 per cent. . . Particular activities qualify for very high rates of incentives, especially under certain grant programs. When the benefits from special tax incentives are added we are looking, in some cases, at an extraordinary generous level of assistance.
Those were the words of the Minister of Finance when he spoke in November, 1984. However, what did he do in May, 1985? He added on a capital gains tax-free amount of $500,000 per individual. We know that that will not benefit someone earning $10,000 or $15,000 per year. It will not help most farmers in western Canada. It will not help people working in the mines or in the forest industry. It will not help people living on a minimum wage or the people who are seeing their family allowances cut back by the Government. What we are dealing with in this Bill is $3.5 billion of extra tax money which the Government proposes to collect from taxpayers to the end of the next fiscal year 1986-87. As is typical with most Government legislation, and it was typical of the Liberal legislation, there is a bit of good news contained in the Bill. There is a minor clause which states that the treatment of the people who are collecting these excise taxes will be more in line with the recent changes to the Income Tax Act. The Department of National Revenue will grant the person who is suspected of withholding taxes improperly the right to make a case for himself or herself and present that case before funds are actually seized from the person's bank account. I mention this clause because it contains good news. The rest of the few minutes which 1 have to speak today on this subject will be with respect to the bad news.
The bad news is that the tax rates which people in Canada have to pay will be going up. Because these are excise taxes and are geared to people who are spending money for consumer goods the load will tend to fall more heavily on lower income people than it will on higher income people. For that reason they should be designated as regressive taxes because they hurt people with average and low incomes far more than they hurt people with higher incomes. The reason for this is quite obvious when one starts going through the list of taxes.

These are items which were exempt from sales taxes previously, such as candy which children buy, soft drinks, pet foods and certain health goods. An 11 per cent tax will be imposed on these items bringing the total cost to consumers up to $990 million- almost $1 billion. That is almost enough to pay for the recent bank bail-out.
Energy conservation equipment did not previously attract any excise tax at all. Taxes will now be imposed on this equipment on the same basis as other consumer items, which raises the question of just how serious the Government is about conservation. The total cost to Canadian consumers in the next fiscal year from these changes, including getting pet owners and children involved in the tax system, will be $785 million. If the concrete is poured on the construction site, labour will not be taxed, but if you decide to build with pre-mixed concrete, a federal tax of 6 per cent will be charged. In announcing this measure, Mr. Speaker, there is something that the Government did not consider, which shows its incompetence and its lack of knowledge about the building industry, since we all know quite well that, in this industry, long-term contracts are signed two or three years beforehand. Last May, it was announced that a 6 per cent tax on pre-mixed concrete would apply from July 1. What happens to the contracts which had already been signed? The Government does not even respect its own commitments regarding this tax.
I have here a letter from the Canada Museums Construction Corporation which concerns a contract signed before the
November 5, 1985

Budget, when there was no 6 per cent federal sales tax. After the Budget, the general contractor wrote to the Corporation asking them to increase his contract, and the answer he got was quite clear: There is no clause in the contract so we cannot act on your request. And now the company has to pay 6 per cent tax on a contract. Well, we all know that the profit margin on these contracts is not that high. The contracts may be big, but the profit margin is very slight. So if the contractor has to pay 6 per cent, Mr. Speaker, we are going to see a number of bankruptcies in the construction industry, a sector that needs stimulating instead of being beaten down by this kind of tax.
Mr. Speaker, 1 could mention the notorious $500,000 capital gains tax exemption. If we look at the statistics for 1982, we see that only 4 per cent of the people who declared capital gains were declaring the kind of gains from industry and businesses that really create jobs. Mr. Speaker, 96 per cent declared capital gains as a result of property transactions and sales of homes and office buildings. They know perfectly well . . . We all know that changing the ownership of a building does not create that many jobs.
Mr. Speaker, instead of saying: We want to stimulate economic recovery, we want to help small businesses invest and create jobs, the Government is giving $500,000 to everyone. With a little bit of accounting imagination, one realizes that these $500,000 could become one million or two million dollars' worth of tax exemptions. So when we say that the Government takes from the poor and people on average incomes and gives to the rich, I know it hurts my hon. colleague, but it is the truth. Obviously, people earning $20,000 per year are not going to have a capital gain of half a million. That is the whole point of this debate, and that is the difference between previous Liberal Budgets and this Progressive Conservative Budget.
I would like to quote some of the organizations which, on the night the Budget was presented, were worried about the Conservative Budget. For example, the Retail Council of Canada was disappointed that a federal sales tax of 1 per cent along with an extension of federal tax on food products was imposed as it will have the greatest impact on lower income Canadians and they will be worse off as they make up the bulk of the consumers. The Consumers Association of Canada said that the average consumer is hard hit with higher expenses, whether through expenditure cuts or increased taxes. The association said that it is hard to imagine how consumers will be encouraged to spend when the money value is reduced.
With regard to the increased consumption taxes, the British Columbia Federation of Labour said that the two-cent increase in gasoline tax to pay for the western energy agreement is a gift to the industry at the expense of the consumer. It said that a consumption tax is regressive by any standard and is a distortion of the tax system.
Excise Tax Act
The Canadian Association of Social Workers said that the Budget was bad news for the lower income population, that it hurts the poor the most and that the child benefit package is another kind of horror. With regard to the reduced child tax exemption it said that there is no indication of where the savings are going. We know that they are going to Canadians who had more than $60,000 on deposit with the Canadian Commercial Bank and to the Reichmann brothers. The Government is giving a $1 billion tax credit to the Reichmann brothers at the same time as it is closing a refinery in the east end of Montreal. The Canadian Association of Social Workers also said that it seems as if we did not care for the low income sector and that we will probably see increases in line-ups at the food banks. We have been seeing that for the past few months, Mr. Speaker.
The National Anti-Poverty Organization said that the Budget is a bad one as far as support to families, the aged and women are concerned. It said that on top of that, all the increased consumption taxes target families directly and will be hardest on those with low incomes who have topay the same for basic products as do the rest. Increased taxes on upper income earners are off-set by giveaways such as the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption. The organization said that this Budget is bizarre as it increases public assistance to those who need it least.

Mr. Speaker, you are signalling that my time has expired. Well, we could go on for quite a while about the Budget and Bill C-80. Unfortunately, our time is limited, and I hope that Canadians will understand what the debate is about today.

subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND RELATED ACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too feel it necessary to participate this morning in the debate on Bill C-80. I feel it necessary because Bill C-80 is, on the whole, a regressive Bill. In simple, layman's terms, effective January 1, 1986 it will increase the sales tax on a wide range of products by 1 per cent. That list of products gives an indication of the regressive element of this Bill and of the mind-set of the Tory Government. It is going to increase the telecommunications programming tax by 6 to 7 per cent. It will increase excise taxes on wines. Federal sales taxes will go up from 10 per cent to 11 per cent. There will be an increase in the gas excise tax of 2 per cent per litre on September 3 and another cent per litre on January 1, 1987. There will be an imposition of sales taxes on carbonated beverages, candy, confectionery and, yes, even pet foods. There will also be a sales tax on health goods and an imposition of sales tax on energy conservation equipment as well as on previously exempt construction and building materials.
We must look at Bill C-80 not only from an economic point of view, but from a social viewpoint as well because it has a dual effect on Canadians, economic and social. On the economic front the Government promised a renewal of the economic spirit in the country. Yet, when you look at this Bill, Mr. Speaker, you have to ask where that spirit is. What kind

November 5, 1985
Excise Tax Act
of economic spirit will impose upon Canadians an increase of S2.6 billion in sales tax alone by 1991? When one couples that with the $4.1 billion increase in income tax imposed by the Budget of last year Canadians begin to ask where the spirit of economic renewal has gone. Where is the spirit of economic fairness in Bill C-80, Mr. Speaker?
It does not take an economic genius to understand that the purchasing power of average Canadians is going to be reduced. It does not take an economist to realize that companies are going to be hard pressed to sell their services and goods at a competitive price. How will this help firms in our country to be more competitive and to sell more products when they have to pass on increased taxes to the consumer?
How will construction companies be assisted by increased taxes on construction commodities and equipment? How will Canadian truckers, who compete with truckers from the United States, feel about this Bill which imposes higher taxes on fuel? How will the tourism industry, which has been lobbying the Government for the last year and a half not to impose higher taxes on gas, react to Bill C-80? How will companies in the energy conservation business react to this Bill which increases the taxes on their equipment? We are saying, on the one hand, that it is important for Canadians to conserve energy, and, on the other hand, we are increasing the taxes on the products that Canadians must purchase and have installed in their homes in order to conserve energy. You simply cannot do both, Mr. Speaker.
This legislation not only squeezes Canadian consumers by decreasing their purchasing power and increasing their taxes, but also squeezes Canadian companies. They are having a tough time as it is making ends meet without having more added to their problems. Clearly, on the economic front, this is a Bill that hits both consumers and companies at the same time.
But there is another element to this Bill that cannot be overlooked. It is its social impact and the social fairness of this particular piece of legislation.
As I mentioned at the start of my speech, I said that it was a regressive Bill. That sentiment is certainly echoed by the Canada Council on Social Development. It estimates that the combination of increased sales, gasoline, alcohol and tobacco taxes will result in tax hikes of $140 for a couple with an annual income of $15,000 in 1990; $282 for a comparable couple with an income of $20,000; and $361 for a couple with an income of $40,000.
We must begin looking at the social equity in this legislation as well. While Canadians will be paying more than $2.6 billion in sales tax alone, the reality is that corporations in this country will enjoy a $2.2 billion tax break. Canadians are asking themselves, and urging the Government to look in the mirror as well, to ask if this is fair economics. Of course, the resounding answer is no. Is it fair to pass increased taxes to the consumer when a very elite community in our country will enjoy capital gains tax breaks that were introduced by the
Minister of Finance last May? Is it fair to pass on to consumers the goal of deficit reduction while the Government is bailing out banks in this country? Is it fair to ask consumers to pay more in the face of the Olympia & Gulf deal of over $1 billion?
Is it fair when tax increases in the Budget introduced by the Minister last May will mean that families in this country which earn $15,000 will pay 35 per cent more tax by 1990 while those earning $200,000 will only pay 4 per cent more and those in the fortunate income bracket of $400,000 will only see an increase of 2 per cent?
What sense of fairness is there in a measure which will mean that a family earning $15,000 will pay 35 per cent more while those earning close to $500,000 will face a 2 per cent increase?
When Government attempted to deindex the pensions of senior citizens, it told pensioners to forget about the social contract they had with the Government because it wanted to reduce the deficit. Is that fair? Of course not, and the senior citizens of the country taught Parliament and the Government in particular a big lesson about fairness. It seems that the Government has not learned its lesson very well because it went on to deindex family allowances. It is essentially telling mothers and children in this country that they also have to bear the brunt of deficit reduction. Yet there are companies and individuals in this country who earn millions of dollars but pay very little or no tax at all.
Canadians realize we must get our financial house in order and they are saying they will do it as long as it is fair for everyone. The $15,000 wage earner is prepared to pitch in with his family to put our financial house in order but he is not prepared to make that sacrifice when other families, individuals and companies in this country are not shouldering a fair burden of deficit reduction for economic renewal.
That is why this Bill is unfair and should not be supported by the House. It does not ask all Canadians to shoulder deficit reduction or the economic renewal equitably. This Bill, like most of the Budget measures, hits those families the hardest who can least afford to pay. That is why a host of organizations have come before Parliament to indicate their disapproval with this Bill. These organizations include the Metro Social Planning Council, COSTI and the Toronto Association of Neighbourhood Services. They have pointed out that this is a regressive and unfair Bill which attempts to place the burden for deficit reduction on the poor.
It is for that reason that the Government should withdraw Bill C-80 and redraft it. It is a regressive Bill which is unacceptable to Canadians.
Therefore, it gives me great pleasure to move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson):
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "that" and substituting the following therefor:
Bill C-80, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act and to
amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be not now read a second time but
that it be read a second time this day six months hence.
November 5, 1985
It is a fair motion that speaks to the equity that all Canadians want in this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, like the Confederation des organismes familiaux du Quebec, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women and more than 90 groups throughout the country, I want to voice my opposition to Bill C-70.
On October 23 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) admitted that the deindexation of family allowances would be used to reduce the deficit, but until then the Conservatives had always maintained that those savings would be set aside for other social programs.
The Government could not care less about its election promises with respect to the social sector, but it does live up to its commitments respecting the energy field, as evidenced by the Western Accord and the dismantling of the National Energy Program.
Bill C-70 has to be one of the measures which has drawn the strongest opposition from family organizations, women's groups and native people associations, among many others. The Conservative Government should be ashamed to bring down upon itself the wrath of poorer Canadians.
When the establishment of a country is in favour of something and the poor try to defend themselves, it is because the Government is not exactly upholding the right cause.
I hope that opposition against the deindexation of family allowances on the part of so many social groups will prompt Members on both sides of the House to have second thoughts.

Mr. Speaker, the process of land claims for Indian bands in Ontario is in much need of repair. The Office of Native Claims is supposed to work in the best interests of Indian people, as is the Department of Indian Affairs whose Minister has a fiduciary responsibility in these matters.
One case in point, where this trust has been abrogated, Mr. Speaker, involves the Stangecoming Band near Fort Frances, Ontario. This Band is situated on an isolated island with no sewer and water, no electricity, no community buildings and, of course, is only accessible by water or air. With only one radio telephone on the island and no schools or medical facilities, it is easy to see why these people want a real place to

November 5, 1985
live. But in order to do so, they need action from the Department of Indian Affairs.
The Minister has been made aware of the situation many months ago by the Stangecoming Band, the Assembly of First Nations, and myself. The Minister is also aware that if this situation is not resolved in a satisfactory manner, the Band will seek redress at a higher level, namely, the Federal Court.
Such action should not be necessary, Mr. Speaker, if the Office of Native Claims and the Minister would adhere to the Indian Act, act in the interest of the Stangecoming Band, and fulfil the commitments undertaken to the Band.

Mr. Speaker, through you, I wish to appeal to the 24 per cent of Canadians who drive automobiles. It is estimated that this many motorists misfuel their cars to save money at the gas pump. Misfuelling occurs when cheaper leaded gas is used in automobiles designed to burn non-leaded fuel exclusively. This practice destroys anti-pollution devices in the engine and causes harmful leaded emissions to be introduced into the air.
I need not remind any Canadian of the evil effects acid rain is having on the environment, our health, and our forests. The short-term gain of a few pennies at the pump is not worth the long-term pain we shall endure if misfuelling continues.
To his credit the federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) has advocated wiping out the price differential between leaded and unleaded gasolines. Better yet, he wants to eliminate lead from gasoline entirely by the early 1990s.
Lest we introduce an Orwellian police state to regulate misfuelling, the onus is on each motorist to control this practice. From this point forward, Mr. Speaker, let each Canadian driver know he or she is part of a nation-wide honor system. Misfuelling must be regarded as a perversion upsetting our fragile environment.

Mr. Speaker, the latest survey made by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business shows that the rising trend in employment and capital investments in the small business sector is firm and that the capital gains tax exemption announced in the May Budget will indeed spur economic growth.
Those measures have restored a climate of confidence and signalled the beginning of a new approach in business planning on the part of many company owners.
The survey reveals that projected increases in capital investments and operating funds are more encouraging than they have been for quite some time.
Mr. Speaker, 42 per cent of those small businesses intend to boost their investment projects in the near future and to hire more people.
Quite clearly, small businessmen have welcomed the measures implemented by our Government to improve the small business investment climate, make funds more readily available, lower interest rates and do away with some of the more redundant regulations governing small businesses.
The survey definitely attests to this Government's intention of leading Canadians on the road to prosperity.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to bring to the attention of the House the plight of retired public servants whose careful planning for their days of much deserved rest has been torn as under by the Government's plan to end full indexing of their pensions.
On April 17 of this year the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) told this House of planned changes to public service pensions. Included in the package of amendments were provisions to replace the present practice of guaranteeing benefits fully indexed against inflation with protection based solely on the earnings of pension funds.
Present superannuates have paid for their pensions and their indexing, and they have every right to expect that protection to continue.
To quote the Progressive Conservative Party's own literature from the last election campaign:
Our position is that current pensioners signed a contract with the Crown in years past and that contract should not be altered unilaterally by government. While our Party recognizes the need to negotiate changes to arrangements with current employees, we are determined that these must not affect the benefits for current superannuates.
If the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act or the Public Service Superannuation Act is changed, a grandfather clause must be introduced to protect former public servants who are now retired. Anything less, Mr. Speaker, would be a betrayal of trust with Canadians who serve our country with diligence and dedication.
November 5, 1985

subsubtopic: NON PAYMENT BY INDIVIDUALS EARNING ABOVE $50,000 ANNUALLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night millions of Canadians from coast to coast tuned in to watch the annual Juno Awards which celebrate excellence in the Canadian music industry.
Today I would like to present the "Golden Loophole Award" for excellence in the field of tax avoidance. Today we learned from Revenue Canada officials that the latest statistics available show that in 1983, 7,782 individual Canadians with incomes above $50,000 per year paid not one red cent in income tax.
When you consider these figures alongside the recent announcements of billion dollar tax breaks for corporations like Olympia & York and Dome Petroleum, it is surprising that taxpayers are not storming the Parliament Buildings.
What is important to remember in all of this, Mr. Speaker, is that this is perfectly legal. If you are wealthy enough to make use of the investment tax credit, the half a million dollar capital gains exemption, the indexed security investment plan or the flow-through share purchase tax credit, to name but a few of these loopholes, it is not surprising that you can end up without having to pay a cent in income tax.
If you are a corporation, Mr. Speaker, it also helps to have a Government formed by either the Liberals or the Conservatives, who have always shown themselves willing to use the taxpayers' chequebook to help out those large corporations that donate so generously to their party coffers.
All in all, I would say that ordinary wage-earning taxpayers are getting tired of having to pay for these tax boondoggles. It is time that the income tax system was changed to require everyone, including the wealthy, to pay their fair share.

subsubtopic: INVESTIGATION OF ALLEGED OVERSPENDING BY CANDIDATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the election expense provisions in the Canada Elections Act have proven, over the past decade, to be an important reform, ensuring that politics in Canada is not a preserve of the wealthy, and providing balance between contending Parties and candidates.
Over the past year, however, those very provisions have themselves proven to stand in need of reform in one important respect. I refer to the investigation of allegations of campaign overspending by candidates.
The Chief Electoral Officer lacks power to investigate complaints, to determine their validity swiftly, fairly, and in an even-handed manner. If he had this power, an investigation could determine whether evidence exists for charges to be laid, and then the matter turned over to the RCMP and made public. Members of all three Parties in the House, and the independent Member, have learned first-hand of the need for a reform of investigative and enforcement powers for election spending, to ensure that equal benefit and equal protection of the law apply to MPs as well as to all other Canadians. We do not need, in the first instance, the heavy hand of an RCMP investigation to determine what is essentially a matter of administrative compliance.
The Mulroney Government has already demonstrated a reform instinct as far as electoral matters are concerned, and I am confident that amendments to the Canada Elections Act could be made here as well.

November 5, 1985

subsubtopic: ABSENCE OF CANADIAN DIMENSION FROM QUEBEC TRADE OFFICE IN NEW YORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I had the honour of being part of the Canadian delegation which visited New York to observe and be briefed on the workings of the United Nations.
Might I say how impressed I was with the Canadian involvement and contribution to the UN. 1 was expecially proud and impressed with our Ambassador, Stephen Lewis, who has breathed new life and enthusiasm into the UN.
As part of our tour we also visited the Canadian Consulate and the Quebec, Ontario and Alberta Trade Offices. Upon entering the Quebec Trade Office I noticed, much to my chagrin, the absence of a Canadian flag. There was not one anywhere to be seen. I thought at first that it was an oversight. When 1 asked why there was not a Canadian flag displayed, I was told bluntly that the office was not there to promote Canada.
On touring the offices, 1 noticed a separatist poster in the office of the administrator. In another office there was an American flag beside a Quebec flag, but no Canadian flag. On reviewing the promotional literature, there was no mention of Canada or the fact that Quebec is a province of Canada.
As a proud Canadian, I felt let down by the Government of Quebec. As a proud Canadian, I felt betrayed. While it may not be the job of the Quebec Trade Office to promote Canada, surely it should recognize Canada as the great united nation we are.

speechtext:
When I spoke yesterday, Mr. Speaker, it was on the closure motion. I indicated that this Party has opposed Bill C-80 because we consider it unfair to low and middle-income earners and also because we think it does not make any economic sense.
It is interesting to find this morning that we got confirmation for this view from the prestigious Conference Board of Canada, which has generally been considered to take a rather conservative viewpoint of economic matters. The Conference Board of Canada points out that the tax increases in the last federal Budget will slow economic growth for the next few years.
In fact, it warns that economic growth will drop to a meagre 1.5 per cent per year, beginning in 1988, as the results of the cumulative measures introduced by the Government takes effect. The Conference Board blames the economic decline which it anticipates on tax increases in the Progressive Conservative Budget of May, which will take away spending money from most Canadians. It indicated that in 1986, the implementation of the more restrictive elements of last May's federal Budget would inhibit the expansion of consumer spending.
When the Government took power, Canada was at a point where it was recovering from a very serious world-wide recession, from which Canadians had been sheltered to some extent by the prudent policies of the previous Liberal Government. Canadians had not suffered as harshly as had people in other countries. Also, the Government inherited some building blocks for recovery and some elements of a good Budget. It has thrown away these advantages. In fact, in Bill C-80 before us we see an attempt, we are told, to grapple with the deficit. However, the attempt takes the form of piling on taxes like Pelion on Ossa on to low and middle income-earners, with the result, as we have heard from the Conference Board of Canada, that the money needed for a consumer-led recovery is disappearing. We will have a dampening of the economy and a dampening of economic growth. In fact, the deficit is more likely to increase.
Among the measures which we see before us in Bill C-80, there are tax increases on gas-two cents per litre in September, 1985, and one cent per litre in January. This will affect farmers. It is certainly already affecting food costs-and we have seen that food costs are up in the last month-because there is an energy cost in every food article. Farmers use energy. It is used for transportation, packaging, storage and retailing. Consumers will have to pay higher food costs as a result of this change.
Many of us have received mail from Canadian trucking companies indicating that the increase will make it more difficult for them to compete with their American competitors. So we see the risk of a loss of Canadian jobs.
A tax is imposed upon many categories of construction material including modular homes, concrete and asphalt. We have all received mail from people in the construction industry who are often locked into fixed cost contracts. For some small and medium-sized construction companies in particular, the fact that they now have to absorb this 6 per cent increase, because they are locked into fixed cost contracts, may mean going out of business. Yet this Government which claims to consult and to be responsive is not even willing to accept what has been proposed by some construction companies, that is, a method of phasing in the sales tax increase so as to allow them to deal with their fixed cost contracts.
Also we see taxes being imposed upon equipment and construction material used in energy conservation. The items which will be taxed at the 11 per cent level as of January 1 include heat recovery units, devices for extracting heat from
November 5, 1985

exhaust air or waste water for the recovery of energy, solar panels and tubes for collecting and converting solar energy, wood burning stoves and space heaters. The items to be taxed at 7 per cent will include thermal insulation.
The Government has clearly made a policy decision to put all its eggs in the oil and gas basket and to discourage Canadians from using alternative forms of energy. Not only that, it is discouraging homeowners who want to save a little money on energy costs by insulating. A price has to be paid for that.
I should like to turn to the sales tax on candy, soft drinks and pet food. Candy manufacturers also asked for time. They were willing to accept the sales tax, but they asked for a little time because many of them had prepackaged and priced their merchandise for their peak sales periods of Hallowe'en and Christmas. They were left with Hobson's choice-either redo the packaging with new prices or absorb the extra cost of the sales tax. The Government has been deaf to their request for a six-month delay.
Turning to the tourism industry, it has very serious concerns about the increase in gasoline tax which it sees as discouraging American visitors who form a large bulk of our tourist trade. That industry foresees a very substantial reduction in the number of American tourists visiting Canada each year, accompanied by a net loss of $135 million to the economy and perhaps over 5,000 jobs, when one takes into account the multiplier factor.
The list goes on and on. The direction is wrong for Canada. The new taxes discourage energy conservation. They impose a very severe hardship upon the construction sector of the economy. When we add the sales tax, higher fuel costs, CMHC cuts and the elimination of the Registered Home Ownership Savings Program to what the construction industry is facing, it is a heavy blow to an industry which was beginning to make a rather nice recovery from the recession.
The total amount to be taken out of the pockets of Canadian consumers in 1990 and 1991 as a result of these sales tax measures and the income tax changes may amount to $6.7 billion. Even this year the amount will be about $2 billion. This can only exert a damaging and dampening effect upon the purchasing power of lower and middle-income Canadians and, therefore, the economy in general.

Mr. Speaker, most of the people I know would rather leave a burning building than rush into it. Most of the people I know would rather say hello to a friend than farewell. Most of the people I know would rather stand in Parliament and speak in favour of a tax reduction rather than tax increases. However, here I am rushing into the burning building to speak in favour of tax increases. I do so because in Bill C-80, the one under debate at this time, there are measures of great importance. I would like in the coming moments to look at three of them.
The first relates to the tax on cigarettes and what it raises in terms of general Government policy for the tobacco culture in our country and our economy. Second is the question of the
Excise Tax Act
tax exemption on certain health goods and what it means for many Canadians, particularly those who are disabled. Third, I should like to touch upon the measures included in Bill C-80 which represent an important step forward in terms of Government financial planning and accountability. I was also encouraged to rise to speak on this Bill because last night 1 heard from the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) who had just returned to Canada from one of the eastern European communist countries. He said that no matter how bad things seemed in Canada, he was awfully glad to get back because in comparison with other countries, things are extraordinarily good here. It would be helpful for Hon. Members to place the relative amount of tax increases contained in Bill C-80 in that broader context. Members should look at them against the backdrop of the sincere effort of the Government to come to grips with the deficit that burdens the country and the future of the country.
Indeed, regarding the deficit, 1 would like to make another preliminary comment. At different times I was thinking about running for Parliament. I looked at the House in the 1960s, that great period of time when Government consisted largely of Ministers rising to announce new spending programs. It was a great expansionist era and politics was relatively easy then because politicians only had to decide what problem faced the country on which they could spend money. That was not hard politics, that was simply a matter of goodwill and the ability to spend money. It is the legacy of that approach which has now returned to haunt us in the eighties, a time when politics has become much harder and involves restraint in an effort to reduce the staggering deficit.
I have listened to the speeches made by Members opposite. As the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Gormley) said this morning, any measure like Bill C-80 is bound to be fodder for the cannons of the Opposition. It is easy to shoot at the Government when tax increases are part of the legislation before us. However, the speeches that have been made in criticism of Bill C-80 have been very big on rhetoric and some of it easy rhetoric, but have not squarely addressed the reality faced by Government in the 1980s.
I now turn to the three measures I wish to mention briefly. One measure designed to increase Government revenue is the tax on cigarettes. This is the second time in the Thirty-third Parliament that a measure has been brought forward to increase tobacco taxes and it is the second time I have risen to speak in support of that increase for the same reason. I believe that the place of tobacco in our culture is something on which it is very difficult to formulate government policy. There are countries like China in which smoking is an indulgence followed by virtually the entire population. This kind of debate would never occur in China. However, in Canada we have now come to a point at which we are recognizing the extraordinary health hazards involved in the use of tobacco as well as the many related costs including the agricultural cost involved in having prime land dedicated to tobacco. A debate is now

November 5, 1985
Excise Tax Act
occurring in Canadian society which goes to the root of what we think of ourselves and how we wish to use certain products.
Hon. Members have recently raised the question of a contradiction in Government policy. Here we are raising tobacco taxes and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has recently announced a spending program that will encourage Canadians and particularly younger Canadians to break the habit of smoking. Contemporaneous to that, there has been a measure of support for tobacco farmers. One could detect here certain inconsistencies.
I believe Government policy is reflecting the state of the debate and the shift in the thinking of Canadian society as a whole. I would hope that in the medium-term, we can move toward a policy that would see agricultural lands now given over to tobacco crops being given over instead to soybean or other crops that are certainly desperately needed in a world in which many people are starving and many more are going to bed hungry every night. I believe we have a broad social responsibility in that area.
Government policy regarding tobacco is clearly now in a state of transition. I hope it can continue along the same line so that within the next five to 10 years, we can see a true transition in the policy toward tobacco and no inconsistency on the part of a Government which is trying to get people to stop using a product that is so destructive to health. If this were to happen, the Government would no longer have the marvellous source of revenue it has from taxing tobacco. There is not a Government in the world that has not turned to levying hefty tobacco taxes in order to raise revenues. However, by the same token, in a society in which the use of tobacco products is alien, many Government expenditures for which those very funds are required including health care costs no longer need to come from the public purse.
The second point I would like to make concerns the tax exemption on certain health goods. I would like to applaud the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) for blending an approach of fiscal responsibility with a compassionate understanding of the needs of Canadians. It did not fall on unhearing ears or to a hardened heart that Canadians, upon hearing plans for removing exemptions from certain products such as those used by diabetics, those who suffer from cardio-vascular diseases and those who suffer from respiratory diseases, requested that the Minister make a change. The Minister announced some weeks ago that the Government is prepared to listen and to modify its policy. As the Chairman of the Committee on Equality Rights, I would hope that the same view will prevail as we look more closely at a number of the tax exemptions available to the handicapped and disabled Canadians.
My final point concerns the effort to bring order and predictability to tax planning in Canada. I support this Bill because it introduces a comprehensive system of assessments, objections and appeals into the Excise Tax Act. This system is similar to the current system under the Income Tax Act and incorporates the recent improvements initiated by the Government in the areas of search and seizure and the presumption of innocence which defer collection and action on taxation until a
taxpayer has had an opportunity to resolve any disputes arising out of his or her tax liability. It is for the same reason that the Government has ended a provision inaugurated by the previous Government regarding the automatic indexation of tobacco taxes. We feel very strongly that it is Parliament that should have the opportunity to debate tax legislation. This point was made this morning by an Hon. Member from Manitoba. Again, I support this legislation because the removal of the automatic indexing of the tobacco tax is a step in the right direction. Whenever it has to be increased it is we here in Parliament, the elected representatives of the people, who will have a chance to speak to it.
