speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have a chance to speak on Bill C-80 which, as all Members of the House know, is nothing more than another regressive tax Bill being dragged forward by the Government because it either does not have the guts or the will to go out and obtain the money where it should. In fact, somewhere between $30 billion and $50 billion could be collected from the corporations of the country. These are taxes which they are legally obliged and required to pay but because of the insufficient will of those who sit on the Government benches those taxes are simply not being collected.
It was interesting to listen to the Hon. Member for Etobi-coke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer). He did not bother speaking about the Little Egypt Bump-the $500 million to $1 billion going to Reichmann's. Instead, he talks about getting tobacco farmers in Canada to grow soybeans, as if those people who are listening to the debate today might think that somehow there is some sort of a comprehensive Government policy with respect to either the question of taxation or the question of tobacco. None of the additional taxes in Bill C-80 will go to help Canadians who are suffering health problems in relation to the fact that they have been either moderate or heavy smokers. In fact, these taxes will go into general revenues to help bail out the corporate friends of the new Government. It is quite clear that those friends are either the banks, the oil companies or certain individuals in Toronto who seem to be receiving the hundreds of millions of dollars which this Government likes to shovel off the backs of the trucks every day.
I would like to deal with how regressive these taxes are because they hit low and middle income earners the hardest, it then goes after the farmers, the fishermen and the forest industry workers in my constituency with a rather vehement beat. It blatantly attacks the tourist industry, as I will demonstrate in a few moments.
Let us consider the key elements coming forward from the May Budget which are contained in Bill C-80. The increases in the federal sales taxes and excise taxes have to be looked at very carefully because, of course, there is an essential difference between the two forms of tax. The sales tax is an ad valorem tax in that it is assessed as a percentage of the price of a good, for example, at 7 per cent, which is simply tacked on. Excise taxes are assessed at a fixed rate, as we recently saw in
November 5, 1985

the first week of September with respect to the 2 cent per litre increase on gasoline. The main thrust of Bill C-80, of course, is to increase revenue though changes in both the scope and rate of the federal sales and excise taxes. There is no question about that. It is somewhere in excess of $3 billion, which point I will come to in a few moments.
There is one interesting point in the Bill for which I think the Government should be supported. I am speaking of the implementation of the presumption of innoncence concept. Although this does not help the overwhelming majority of taxpayers in the country who have their taxes lobbed off every two weeks, and who never really get an opportunity to use the clause, for some small business people and for fishermen, farmers and truck loggers in my constituency, it will be a rather useful change to the tax legislation.
The major increases in the Bill are as follows. The federal sales tax will be increased by 1 per cent effective January 1, 1986. Therefore, the new rate will be 7 per cent on construction materials. I know that will not help speed up the number of housing starts in the country. There will be a 7 per cent tax levied on cable and pay television services, which will certainly not help those people who are either in long-term care facilities or who are shut in at home for long periods of time for whatever reason. It will certainly hit low and middle income people much harder than anyone else. There will be a 14 per cent tax increase on alcoholic beverages and on tobacco products and an 11 per cent increase on other taxable goods. The total with respect to these increases in relation to Bill C-80 will be $990 million in fiscal year 1986-87 which will be borne directly by the taxpayers.
One initiative which has been fought consistently across the country and which has received a few rather narrow changes to it is the concept of broadening the sales tax base. The historic exemptions for candy, confectionary goods, soft drinks, pet foods and certain health goods are still basically in place. There have been some minor changes by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in this respect. However, one which I find particularly irritating and one which is an example of colossal government stupidity is the broadening of the sales taxes to include energy conservation equipment. Studies which have been done by the National Research Council, by many provincial Governments and by many independent environmental organizations in the country demonstrate that that stands to be one of the stupidest things which has been done by the Government and one which will be hard felt in years to come as we see energy costs rising. This will be compounded by the fact that we will have used up so much more of our non-renewable energy base. To cut off funding to the scientific study of alternate energy, as we have seen at the NRC, and to cut back funds to universities and independent organizations across the country, whether it be with respect to wind, solar, biomass or any other alternate energies, is an example of a Government which his clearly in the pockets of the oil patch. Unfortunately for Canadians the Government is closing off one of the most promising small business enterprises which we have seen in this decade. Anyone who takes the time to study
Excise Tax Act
the figures would be quite astonished at the number of jobs which have been created and the long-term energy and cost savings both to the environment and to the economy. Those people could not find this concept of the Minister of Finance to be anyhting but stupid. The cost of this broadening will be some $785 million directly to the end of fiscal year 1986-87. It is interesting to note that not one single Member on the Government side has touched on the changes to the energy conservation area and what the impact will be in terms of job losses. We know that there will be almost $1 billion more in taxes on that sector; but no one from the government side has pointed out the large number of jobs which will be lost by so blatantly attacking a young and innovative new enterprise in Canada.
The excise tax will be increased on the following goods. Effective September 3, as we have already seen, an additional two cents a litre on gas and aviation gas had a hard felt impact on a constituency such as mine, which is about one-third of British Columbia, where many truck loggers are already hauling 200 miles each way in some cases. It does not take too many of these two cent a litre bumps to put many of these people practically out of business. We have seen the same thing occur with respect to many of the smaller airlines because there was already an increase of two cents a litre on diesel and aviation fuel. The Government sort of buries away and hides some of these increases, which is one reason I suppose we went metric with respect to gasoline. It is easier to hide from Canadian consumers just how great a lot of these jumps are in terms of taxation because of the change from gallons to litres. I see a resident expert on metric nodding knowingly from the government benches. I hope he will stand up and fight against this Bill. There is another one cent per litre on gas and aviation fuel effective January 1, and another cent per litre on diesel fuel and aviation fuel. The cost of these fuel tax increases to the end of 1986-87 will be $1,325 billion.
It is interesting that the Minister of Finance has not tabled in the House what the effect of this type of increase in taxation will be on farmers, fishermen, truck loggers, trucking companies and all those small airlines which fly not only in northern British Columbia but throughout Canada. I really object to this type of across-the-board taxation being brought in without knowing what the impacts will be.
When it comes to tourism I think the figures which I can put before the House will make it clear that these types of taxation increases are damaging some of the key industries in the country. The various per unit taxes on alcohol, with an increase of 2 per cent, and on cigarettes, with an increase of one cent per cigarette, are quite different. None of that money will go directly to deal with one of the most serious health problems not only in Canada but in the western world which is related to the consumption of cigarettes. There has been no serious attempt by the Government to deal in a comprehensive way with the issue of tobacco. The cost in this respect to the end of fiscal year 1986-87 is $440 million. Just on alcohol and tobacco alone we can see the Government stretching its long fingers into everyone's pockets on a fairly regular basis. The

November 5, 1985
Adjournment Motion
cost to the Canadian consumer with respect to these excise tax increases comes to $1,765 billion. When combined with the other hidden costs which the Minister of Finance has brought in to the end of next year it will amount to another $3.54 billion. I am sorry I do not have time to speak about tourism. However, let me conclude by quoting briefly from a speech of the Minister of Finance which demonstrates quite clearly how taxes in the last 10 years have gone from the individual taxpayer paying 50 per cent and corporations paying 50 per cent to corporations now paying 25 per cent and individuals paying 75 per cent. If we follow that through to the year 2000, individual taxpayers will pay it all. The Minister of Finance said on November 28, 1984, and I quote:
Our recent figures indicate that the effect of tax incentives has been to reduce the average federal corporate income tax rate from 36 per cent to 15 per cent... Particular activities qualify for very high rates of incentives, especially under certain grant programs. When the benefits from special tax incentives are added we are looking, in some cases, at an extraordinary generous level of assistance.
It is clear that the Minister of Finance, and the new Government, are giving all the give-aways to the rich and to the corporations and are loading all the taxes, particularly these kinds of taxes, on to low and middle income earners and are bankrupting many small businesses across the country.

speechtext:
I am just delighted to have a chance to speak on Bill C-80 because it is a Bill which clarifies the fact that the Government is out to deceive the people and will certainly not keep its election campaign promises. I simply point to the two cents excise tax which was imposed on farmers, fishermen, forestry workers and on the mining industry on September 3 of this year.
During the election campaign last year the Government made a very strong promise that it was going to reduce taxes for farmers, fishermen, forestry workers and for the mining industry. On November 8 of last year it did reduce the excise tax by some three cents. It also gave an exemption to the petroleum compensation charge of 1.8 cents. On June 1, that exemption from the petroleum compensation charge of 1.8 cents a litre was eliminated but the price of gasoline did not go down. On September 1, the two cents excise tax was implemented so we see a new expensive tax loaded onto Canadian farmers. In fact, it is estimated that that tax will cost farmers something like $130 million. On top of that, there will be an additional tax of one cent on fuel starting January 1, 1987. At the end of December of next year the three cents excise reduction which has been in effect will be wiped out. Therefore, we will see farmers, fishermen, forestry workers and mining companies paying the full shot, plus a couple of extra cents per litre. This shows the kind of double dealing activity for which the Government is becoming famous.
The Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer) spoke this afternoon about the tobacco tax and tobacco farmers. If he is really interested in defending the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), he should visit St. Thomas this weekend. It is expected that 1,000 farmers will rally in St. Thomas to call the Government to account for its lack of action in agriculture. No industry has suffered more than the farmers from the farm debt crisis this past year, especially the young farmers. Yet the Government has failed to act. In fact, by this nine cents a gallon excise on gasoline, it is imposing even greater hardship on the agricultural community.
The Ontario Government changed from a Conservative Government to a Liberal Government last July and within a matter of two or three weeks, in the Budget brought down the provincial Government provided $50 million in relief for the farmers of Ontario. That is the kind of action which this Minister of Agriculture should be taking. Last year he put a moratorium on farm foreclosures. The situation has worsened.
November 5, 1985

We now have 23 per cent of our farmers, instead of 19 per cent, in serious financial difficulty and we see no action.
The Farm Credit Corporation was reduced from some $494 million of farm assistance, long-term loan funding, to only $90 million this year. On July 10 of this year, the Minister promised to bring in legislation on an urgent basis this fall with amendments to the Bankruptcy Act to provide a pre-foreclosure, pre-bankruptcy arbitration procedure for young farmers facing foreclosure. He started to walk away from this promise in September. Last week he was at the point where he was saying he would seriously consider it. This kind of lack of action is the reason the Minister of Agriculture is going to have to face many hundreds of young farmers in serious financial difficulty this Saturday when he goes home to his riding.
This Government has billions and billions of dollars. It has a $1 billion for a write-off for the Reichmann brothers in Toronto. It has $1 billion for Petro-Canada to buy 1,800 gasoline stations and refineries. But the Government has no money for farmers. This Bill exacerbates their situation because it imposes an additional two cents a litre, or nine cents a gallon, on farm fuel costs. It is a deliberate back-tracking and contravention of the very promises which the Government made. The Government imposes this tax at a time when the harvest is getting into full swing in western Canada. It is a travesty. It is unfair and unjust. On top of that the Government is going to impose an additional one cent sales tax on all farm supplies, including gasoline, which will probably cost a little over one cent a gallon. It will be imposing it on all farm supplies and goods.
The Government promised agri-bonds, long-term low-interest rate funding for farmers. It reneged on its promise. The Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs made a strong recommendation that we have an agri-bond program to help young farmers who are facing serious financial difficulty, but there was no action about that whatsoever in the Budget. The Government promised to revise Section 31. There was no action there. It promised to expand agricultural research and development. Yet the Government is cutting back $50 million on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. That is reputed to be coming out of the research budget. The Government is reneging on its promise of an agricultural research institution in Quebec. The Toxicology Centre at the University of Guelph, which would have been very valuable to agriculture, was cut by the former Minister of the Environment. She did not have a clue about anything in the environment but you would think she would have at least learned something about that institution before cancelling it. suggests a kind of arrogance that one would have thought the Government would have taken longer in coming to. I know that coming to the House of Commons with 211 Members was a very, very heady sensation. The actions of the Government over the past year and other errors of omission, shall we say, which were committed, surely reflect the fact that the Government was so very sure in its numbers that it felt it could do anything. With much less than 211 Members it can, under the present rules, restrict debate and force us to express ourselves by voting against a matter, but in fact allow the measure to be carried through.
The traditions of Parliament are very, very strong. There are any number of Members of past Conservative caucuses who are spinning in their graves these days as they contemplate a Government bringing in time limitation motions and forcing matters to a vote, taking them out of the hands of Members of the House of Commons. It is not any kind of illegitimate use of the position of an Opposition member to oppose an action of the Government if one thinks it is unwise. There is abundant reason for saying that the tax measures with which we are faced in this particular Bill are unwise. Given that, we have a positive duty to the people of Canada to object to this measure with all the energy we have, knowing always that the rules of the House of Commons now impose very severe constraints on us. Particularly when we are few in number in the House, the possibility of our debating measures indefinitely is obviously very, very limited.
I suppose members of the Government might say that we are few in number because that is what the Canadian people thought of us on September 4 and therefore we should be quiet and let them govern the country as they see fit. Of course, the Canadian people do not see things quite that way any longer. Many, many Canadians know that on September 4, 1984 they made a very serious mistake. I think they are quite supportive of us in criticizing the Government's actions, as is, in fact, our constitutional responsibility, and in pointing out the weaknesses of the programs which the Government has put forward.
1 have suggested, Mr. Speaker, that what the Government has put before us in Bill C-80 is a mistake. Members in the Government caucus argue that the deficit had to be dealt with. I will not deny the truth of that proposition. It is a question of how to do it. What members of the Government, private Members included, do not talk about is one of the brute realities which the Auditor General of Canada has pointed out, that is, that the federal Government neglects to collect large amounts of taxes due to provisions such as those of the accelerated capital cost allowances which allow companies to avoid taxes. In just the past weeks we have seen some examples of that sort in the provisions which the Olympia & York interests were able to exploit to acquire Gulf Oil. More recent revelations of the Auditor General indicated provisions which Dome Petroleum was allowed to use earlier this year which will allow it to escape paying hundreds of millions of dollars of taxes.

If in fact the Auditor General is correct in saying that the total of the taxes which are not paid year after year is $35 billion to $50 billion, then I do not understand how any Conservative who can think straight and add and subtract does not realize that the deficit is in fact a result of the tax laws of the country. There are people who are bearing the burden of taxation because the Conservative Government, which felt the same way as the Liberal Government did in the past, has refused to take large and effective action and has left the burden of taxation on individuals and small businesses while large business gets away with all kinds of tax breaks. Some solemn shaking of the head will not change the reality that if the total tax revenue that is not received exceeds $35 billion it will be more than equivalent than the entire deficit in the current Budget. Those Members who do not see the country from the Bay Street perspective will appreciate that if the Government does not close that collection of loopholes it will have no choice but to do exactly what is provided for in Bill C-80 and other measures. The Government will decide to tax the little people in Canada, the individuals, families and small businesses, while the wealthy and large businesses in this country will escape the burden of taxation.
Many Conservative Members will not be back to the next Parliament of Canada. Those Members will want to think about that because in their communities across the country, from Erie to Fraser Valley West and all the way to the East Coast, there are people who will realize that they will have less money to spend next year. They realize that the small businesses in their communities which depend totally on the people in those communities with whom they do business will suffer because of a decline in business.
There are those Members who believe that the way to create a prosperous Canada is to lower the deficit by cutting the expenditures on the one hand while increasing taxes on the little people, including small business and low and middle income Canadians. Those Canadians will say that they did not get the change for which they voted on September 4. Rather, they will see that they got another dose of Liberal Government as far as taxes are concerned and, therefore, ought to look elsewhere. It will be obvious to those Canadians that the old line Parties are exactly as described by predecessors in my Party and caucus over the years. They are Tweedledum and Tweedledee. As David Lewis would say occasionally, I believe, they are Tweedledum and Tweedledumber.

In 1983, Canada had a record travel deficit, and an important cause of this deficit is the much higher price of gasoline in Canada compared to the United States.
Another Member said on January 30, 1984 and I quote:
The Canadian Automobile Association states that the high cost of gasoline has been a major culprit in deterring foreign travellers from auto touring in Canada. About 85 per cent of all tourism in Canada is by automobile.
Another Member said, and I quote:
The tourist industry is definitely pessimistic. We could take steps to reverse the trend in this crucial sector, and we would be well advised to start by reducing the federal tax on gasoline.
Those statements were made by Conservative Members when they were in the Opposition. I have yet to hear those Members raise the same points in the debate on Bill C-80.

The paper is about the consultation process leading up the National Conference on Tourism for Tomorrow, and it says that more than 1,000 private citizens, businesses, professional associations and specialized groups in Canada gave their views on the problems being experienced by the Canadian tourist industry and the industry's potential. The 1,000 respondents said time and time again that current prices in Canada were too high, especially compared with the United States, and that this was very bad for tourism. Most comments were about the price of gas and alcoholic beverages.
Mr. Speaker, that is what our respondents had to say about the prices and more specifically about the price of spirits and gasoline. And here is what Bill C-80 brings us when we look at the price of spirits and gasoline, which are two major factors for the tourist industry.
Mr. Speaker, I may say, first of all, that the tourist industry is a very important one for Canadians. Tourism generates thousands of jobs. There are 600,000 persons working in this sector, which means that one out of ten Canadians work in the tourist industry. The industry represents 5 per cent of our gross national product and generates revenues of approximately $20 billion, which means it is well ahead of many other industries.
Mr. Speaker, nevertheless, despite the importance of this sector, the Government is doing everything it can to harm an industry that could create the jobs we need today.

It also provides for an increase of 2 cents per litre in the tax on gasoline, diesel fuel and airplane fuel, as of September 3. We also find an increase of 1 cent per litre, effective January 1, 1987. The House will recall that the purpose of this increase is to pay for the full indexation of pensions for the elderly. The legislation also provides for extending sales tax to candy and soft drinks, pet food and certain health care products, which of course goes beyond the concerns of the tourist industry. We also find in this Bill the 1 per cent increase in sales tax, effective January 1, 1986.
So, to get back to the tourist industry: If we consider the price of spirits, we find that the Canadian Government is levying three times as much tax on a bottle of spirits as the U.S. Government.

Mr. Speaker, I shall if I may get back to the price of gasoline, which is the most important consideration for people who come to visit this country by car. PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   ELECTORAL BOUNDARIES READJUSTMENT ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SEPARATE REPRESENTATION FOR LABRADOR
speechtext:
that Bill C-228, an Act respecting the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present this Bill on behalf of many people from the area known as Labrador. In their presentation to Hon. Members of all three Parties, the residents of Labrador explained that they feel they need a separate seat to represent their interests in the House of Commons. They point to the special dispensation we have at the present time for Prince Edward Island, the two seats we have at the present time for the Northwest Territories and the seat we have for Labrador. In talking with Hon. Members of all three political Parties, they have made a point that Labrador is a distinct geographical entity with clearly defined borders. It stands historically, culturally, socially, logistically and politically apart from the rest of the province.
Labrador has the special geographical consideration and special community considerations which have allowed similar dispensations for Prince Edward Island, the Yukon and the Territories.
Precedent already exists under the Constitutional Acts of 1867, 1982 and special Clauses 51(a) Subsection 1 and Rule 6, Subsection 2. Labrador, already difficult to serve because of its geography, must share representation with mainland Newfoundland. The purpose of this Bill is to provide full and exclusive representation for that part of the province. In making my presentation, Mr. Speaker, I do so with the realization that it has little chance of being passed within the next 35 minutes. However, I do believe the people of that region of Canada deserve to have their concerns studied by the Committee on Privileges and Elections of this House of Commons. As you know, Mr. Speaker, at the present time the Committee on Privileges and Elections is looking into a redistribution Bill which was presented to this House by the Government House Leader. It is my intention, in making this speech in the House of Commons today-and hopefully other Hon. Members will indicate their support for this particular motion-that we ask the Committee on Privileges and Elec-
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act tions, on which I serve, to look into the special problems which are faced by the people of that section of the province.
As someone who comes from a large northern riding-and I am sure the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) feels the same way-we understand the difficulties which a Member of Parliament has in getting around in a large geographical riding where there are no roads between communities and communities quite often have a small population and are spread out. What we are asking is not a blank cheque for the creation of a new seat for the House of Commons, but that the peculiar situation in which the people of Labrador find themselves be investigated by a Committee of the House of Commons and that we do all we can to try to meet the needs and concerns of the people from that region.
I am not going to take the full 20 minutes which would be allotted to me to speak on this Bill because there have been two votes and we only have 40 minutes left for the entire debate. What I will do in the next few minutes is to point out some of the things which have happened in the past. The idea of a separate seat for Labrador is not something which came from one political Party. It is not something which came from the New Democratic Party, the Conservative Party or the Liberal Party. What this is is a response to the efforts of the people of that region. They have founded a committee and that committee has written to people of all political Parties in the last few years. It is a committee which is asking for a seat encompassing the actual area of Labrador. They have written to the Premier of that province and he has indicated support for the concept. They have written to the representatives of the Liberal Party who have supported that concept. They have written to the New Democratic Party and our representative in the House of Assembly there has indicated his support for this proposal. Therefore this is something which has the support, if not officially of all three parties, nevertheless, the support of representatives of all three Parties. I believe it is certainly worthy of study and I would encourage Hon. Members of the House of Commons to indicate their support for this piece of legislation or at least indicate that they are willing to have the committee study particular problems of the people of that region.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have a chance to make some comments on Bill C-228 brought before the House by the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy). It was interesting to hear some Churchillian statements about the need to have adjustments for the electorate in Labrador.
8390

November 5, 1985
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act
To place this very important recommendation contained in Bill C-228 in a certain context, I would like to turn to several very relevant and timely documents. The first of those is the report of the study group which met at Halifax on September 25 to 27. This is the study group of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association. It was my honour to be the chairman of that study group. Subsequent to the Halifax meeting the report was represented in Saskatoon before the full CPA Meeting. There appears at page 27 the observation that those Government officials charged with the limitation of electoral boundaries are at times accused of being concerned only with the numbers and of ignoring other factors such as community of interest, community of identity or historical patterns. Since a realistic tolerance level may be difficult to establish, these other factors may have to be given more emphasis. On page 28 of that same report, the conclusion of the delegates was expressed as the view that in redistributing electoral boundaries, equality of representation should be one of the main guiding principles. The principle of one vote, one value, should be uppermost while not precluding consideration of the political, legal and institutional factors. Those are the considered opinions of Parliamentarians from many Commonwealth countries who looked at the same subject which has been raised in Bill C-228, a Bill which would reflect and, indeed, recognize that Labrador has a distinct geographical entity with clearly defined borders and that it stands historically, culturally, socially, logistically and politically apart from the rest of the province, Newfoundland.
That brings us to the fact that, as the Hon. Member for Churchill has noted, the Government, acting through the Government House Leader, has brought forward legislation which will deal with redistribution of the constituencies in this Parliament. Bill C-74, to which I am referring, is at this stage before committee and will be reported back to this House by November 26. This is an important Bill because it not only amends the formula for deciding the number of seats in this House found in Section 51 of the Constitution Act, it would amend the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, which is more relevant to the point raised in the Hon. Member's Bill. It would do so by providing to those commissioners who have the task of dividing up the boundaries in each province the power to depart in extraordinary cases from the 25 per cent rule. As Hon. Members know, the wording of the Act is that the population of each electoral district shall correspond as nearly as may be to the electoral quota for the province. That is to say, the quotient obtained by dividing the population of the province as ascertained by the number of Members of the House of Commons to be assigned to the province. We are suggesting two things in Bill C-74. First, that we change the wording "as nearly as may be" to "as close as reasonably possible". So we are, as the first step, introducing a doctrine of reasonableness. Second, we are amending the section to provide the possibility of going above or below the 25 per cent tolerance in extraordinary cases.
I think, Mr. Speaker, there can be no better example of an extraordinary case than that of Labrador. I am advised by one of my colleagues from Newfoundland that Labrador contains four, perhaps four and a half, electoral districts. Certainly it has a number of representatives in the provincial House, but at the federal level it is of course linked with one of the Newfoundland proper constituencies. The new provision being brought before Parliament in Bill C-74 will allow for the kind of suggestion that the Hon. Member for Churchill has made. That is why when he says here, as he did a few moments ago, that perhaps the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections should look into the possibility of doing something like this, I would like to reassure him that we have done more than look into the possibility; the Government has brought in legislation which will permit the very kind of thing he advocates. Therefore, I draw from those comments the inevitable inference that the Hon. Member for Churchill will be fully supportive of Bill C-74, not only as it goes through committee but when it comes back to the House for a vote.
If I may be permitted a further point, I was reviewing the book I wrote four years ago entitled Political Rights, in which I talk about the quality of representation. I would make a final observation concerning the long-heard expression of one man, one vote, or one vote, one value. There is no question that in a parliamentary democracy such as ours that is a fundamental concept. However, as important as that doctrine may be, it is not the only doctrine relevant here. It is one of two, the second being the doctrine concerning the quality of representation. The concept of one vote, one value, means each of us must represent as closely as possible the same number of electors. At the same time an equally important reality is the quality of that representation. At that Commonwealth Parliamentary Conference in Saskatoon which I referred to a few moments ago, and the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) was there, we heard the very powerful speech by an Australian parliamentarian who said that democracy does not belong to Parliament or the Members of Parliament or the Government or any of the institutions, it belongs to the people. It is not a democracy if the people who live in concentrated urban areas can have ready access to their Member of Parliament any day of the week, any time they want to raise their questions and concerns, whereas in other parts of the country men and women have to wait weeks and perhaps months before the MP comes around to their community and talks to them personally to receive their representations, concerns, and proposals. We do have a geographically scattered population and, as the Hon. Member for Churchill indicates in the Bill before us now, that reality must be recognized in the way we distribute the constituencies.
If this exercise was nothing more than a mathematical computation, we could simply add up the Canadian population and have a computer tell us where the electoral boundaries should be. However, that is not the exercise which is involved when electoral boundaries are delineated. It is, rather, a delicate balancing act which seeks to take into account a
November 5, 1985

number of important factors, not the least of which is the accessibility of MPs to their electors, as well as having constituencies of a manageable size so that MPs can readily get around them to see those people they represent.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the idea contained in this Private Members' Bill is a very important one. It is one which has already occurred to the Government and is fully reflected in the new provisions which will be part of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act once Bill C-74 becomes law. For that reason I am sure the Hon. Member for Churchill will be exceedingly supportive of these initiatives by the Conservative Government to deal with a fundamentally difficult issue courageously so that long overdue reform of our electoral system is actually addressed, and so that the quality of representation comes closer to reality.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   ELECTORAL BOUNDARIES READJUSTMENT ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE SEPARATE REPRESENTATION FOR LABRADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say that I think the present quality of our representation is excellent, it could not be any better, covering the Labrador district. Let me also say that people in areas like Labrador sometimes wonder how it is that they, with a population of
30,000,	cannot have a seat unto themselves where they are geographically removed from Newfoundland. They look at another area of Canada which has less population in a federal seat and ask why they cannot have a separate seat. It makes much more sense for an area such as Labrador with a population of 31,000 to be designated as a separate seat than it does for some other areas of the country with less population to be designated as separate seats. Of course, Mr. Speaker, it goes back to the Constitution which states that you must have an amount of seats at least equal to the number of Senators that represent a particular province.
It was good news to hear the Government Member say a few moments ago that with the passage of Bill C-74 this very issue will be addressed by the Government of Canada. I do not know whether we can conclude from that that Labrador will get an extra seat through action of the Government, but it is certainly good news to hear the Hon. Members say, on behalf of the Government, that that problem will be addressed.
I think there is perhaps value in pointing out to the Chamber the reason an area such as Labrador deserves, in a way, to be treated differently than other areas of Canada. There is nothing strange about Labrador. Labrador is the same as Gander-Twillingate is in Newfoundland. Parts of Labrador have the finest facilities to be found anywhere. Labrador City is a modern community. However, due to the geographic location of Labrador, it has certain problems not experienced in any other part of Canada.
With regard to one of the problems, I could never figure out why, in our so-called social security safety net, we have rules based on times of year. There are fishermen all along the coastline of Labrador. The law states that the fishing season will run from May 15 to November 1. That is a strange rule to have in northern Canada because the ice is on shore after May 15. Consequently, the Canadian fishery can be operating all
Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act along the coastline of Quebec, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, but it cannot operate on May 15 of the Labrador Coast. That has a very important effect, Mr. Speaker. By law unemployment insurance for fishermen is cut off on May 15. What do you do if the ice is on the coastline and you cannot get out to fish on May 15 or June 15?
People who live in areas like Labrador have problems distinct from those in any other northern part of the country. Fishermen ask why they are treated the same as people in the so-called southern areas which you, Mr. Speaker, may call northern areas. Their question should be addressed by the Minister in charge of unemployment insurance who has commissions on-going in an attempt to find out what to do with unemployment insurance. Well, Mr. Speaker, those fishermen could tell her what to do with unemployment insurance. The answer is quite simple. You must treat fishermen like everyone else and then solve the problem on the Labrador coast. If a fisherman could draw unemployment insurance as a normal labourer does, that is, after a 10 or 20-week qualifying period, the problem would be solved. Perhaps that is too simple for the Government of Canada to see. Perhaps it is a little bit too straightforward and sensible for the commissions that are set up to re-examine the present unemployment insurance system. This is a case of outright discrimination against these people.
There is the other problem, Mr. Speaker, of weather. Federal-provincial relations are sometimes very important with regard to areas like Labrador. The Member of Parliament for Grand-Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey) was recently working on the problem of the installation of water and sewer facilities in Labrador. As often happens, about four or five months ago the federal and provincial Governments did not agree and the construction season has passed in certain areas on the Labrador coastline.
I suppose that these are some of the factors that went into the decision of the Hon. Member to introduce this Bill, if we interpret some of his explanatory notes correctly. He does say in the Bill that he would make Grand Falls-White Bay a separate riding with a population of 47,559. I do not agree with that. He would make Labrador a separate riding with a population of 31,318. I agree with that. I think we should allow the Bill to pass and then let the boundaries commission decide what the remaining districts in the Province of Newfoundland should be. Certainly the Hon. Member would not suggest that we should have a separate riding with a population of 47,559 when my riding is next door with almost double that population.
However, to facilitate matters, I suggest that we should pass the Bill through the Chamber this afternoon, as I am sure the Government is going to agree with it. We can then ask the boundaries commission to divvy up the remaining ridings in the Province of Newfoundland. Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, that if the Government had allowed the redistribution to take place, there would have been an extra seat in Newfoundland and Labrador. However, the Government insists that we continue to have seven ridings in Newfoundland and Labrador

I take my hat off to the Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador who has done such a magnificent job on behalf of Labrador over the years.
IVfr. Keith Penner (Cochrane-Superior): Mr. Speaker, I agree with my hon. friend, the Member for Gander-Twillin-gate (Mr. Baker) who said that we ought to move quickly to pass this Bill and send it to a committee for further study. I would like to commend the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) for bringing to the attention of the House an anomaly which ought to be corrected. Since redistribution is now under active consideration, this is an ideal time to do it.
I would like to say, by way of preface, that it was my privilege a number of years ago to travel with the Hon. Member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Romp-key) in the part of his constituency that is designated as Labrador. It was a never to be forgotten experience for me. The difficult aspects of moving from place to place along that coast are deeply imprinted in my mind. For example, I recall being weathered in for four days at a place called Marys Harbour. Being weathered in there was different from what I or the Hon. Member for Churchill are accustomed to. Being weathered in usually means that there is a low ceiling or fog which makes it difficult for aircraft to come in and pick up passengers. In the case of Labrador, we were weathered in because of the extraordinarily high winds. On a number of occasions the aircraft we were using took to the air but made no progress at all because of the strong head winds. We had to come back for another day of waiting. That illustrates the difficulty a Member of Parliament has in representing a constituency with those conditions which face him or her regularly.
I listened with great care to the Hon. Member for Etobi-coke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer) in this debate because he is certainly the resident expert on matters related to redistribution and matters related to all electoral laws. I want to commend him very highly for the work he performed on behalf of all of us at a meeting of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association earlier this year in Halifax to do a special study on problems related to electoral law. According to all reports that I have received, his contribution was outstanding.
The Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore was absolutely correct when he said that the way in which the House of Commons represents a country cannot simply be a numbers fame that is arrived at by the use of a computer. The House of Commons must reflect, as accurately as possible, the nature and reality of our nation. This cannot be done by simply allowing representation by population to be the one and only guiding principle. We know this because we have already taken a number of steps with legislation in the past in order that more accurate or fairer representation could be given. For example, I draw to the attention of the House the fact that a few years ago we decided to introduce legislation allowing the
Northwest Territories to have a second seat. It simply was not realistic to have one constituency that included the western Arctic and all of the eastern Arctic. It made no sense at all. Therefore, the Northwest Territories is represented by two Members of Parliament. It would be unthinkable not to have the Yukon Territory represented. How would the House or Parliament ever be what it is if we did not have representation from the Yukon Territory? The Hon. Member for Churchill tells us that there is an anomaly in Labrador. I agree and I think we should move to correct it by the adoption of Bill C-228.
In concluding, I want to remind the House that my hon. friend, the Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) has been giving serious consideration to a Bill that would allow the aboriginal people in northern Quebec, those people who come under the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement, to have representation in the House. They are the Cree of northern Quebec, the Naskapis people of northern Quebec and the Inuit. There should be a seat in the House of Commons in order to represent those people who in fact live under a treaty which we ratified in the House and which puts them into regular contact with the Government of Canada. They have no spokesperson of their own and 1 would support that Bill from the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East in the same way that I can support this Bill by the Hon. Member for Churchill. In the same vein, there is a situation in northern Ontario which I believe would justify a seat under exactly the same principle. The Nish-nawbe-Aski nation, which lives north of 50 degrees and occupies a territory which stretches from the Quebec border almost to the Manitoba border, do not have their own spokesperson in the House of Commons. It would make eminently good sense if that were a designated constituency for the purpose of representation in the House of Commons.
The Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore was quite correct in drawing our attention to the Bill introduced by the Government, Bill C-74, which says that the Commission may, in extraordinary circumstances, depart from the 25 per cent more or 25 per cent less of the electoral quota for the province. Indeed, that does give the Boundary Commission powers an opportunity to respond to legitimate briefs and representations that they did not have before. Nevertheless, 1 still believe that we should follow the practice that we followed in the past in the case of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, to provide legislation to give the Commission more direction and greater certainty. They could be told that although they have these powers under the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act, we believe that Labrador ought not be ignored, that the aboriginal people of northern Quebec ought not to be ignored and that the Indian people who are part of the Nishnawbe-Aski nation, the treaty nine configuration in northern Ontario, ought not to be ignored either.

subtopic: TRADE-PROTECTIONIST MEASURES PROPOSED IN UNITED STATES CONGRESS
TRADE-PROTECTIONIST MEASURES PROPOSED IN UNITED STATES CONGRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to follow up on my question of October 29 concerning the proposed trade negotiations with the United States. My question on that day was to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) concerning the potential problem of trade protectionism in the United States.
Adjournment Debate
We have been assured through the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that President Reagan would exercise his veto should extreme steps of protectionism arise in that country. The Secretary of State assured me of that.
Just going back a little, Mr. Speaker, on September 26, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) recommended to the Government that Canada begin trade negotiations with the United States at the earliest possible moment. Subsequent to that, the Prime Minister announced in this House that we would be sitting down with our ally, the United States of America, to begin the process of trade negotiations.
I would like to highlight the four steps involved in the process with the U.S. The first one we have already covered, that it is really the Minister for International Trade and the U.S. trade representative who submit their reports in accordance with the Quebec trade declaration.
Second, Congress has authority over tariffs. The administration cannot seek negotiating authority from Congress until it receives a proposal for trade negotiations from another country. That is the step we have taken.
Third, a formal proposal is required by letter from either the Prime Minister or the Minister for International Trade expressing our willingness to enter into negotiations of a trade agreement which would include tariff reductions.
Fourth, the administration sends the request for negotiations to Congress, which has 60 calendar days to consider the request. If Congress does not disapprove within this period, the administration may proceed to negotiations. There is no time limit in which the negotiations must be completed. That process has now begun.
I had the privilege to serve as an alternate on the special joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate on the subject of trade enhancement with the U.S. this past summer. We heard witnesses in Halifax, Montreal and in Toronto. Clearly, there are a number of concerns about this important topic. It may well be one of the most important decisions this Government makes. I suggest we should approach it with vigour and optimism but also knowing that we are up against a major ally which has some serious trade problems. That is not to say we should take anything away from what we are trying to do.
May I highlight the four objectives the Government has in mind. They include: security of access, expanded access in the U.S., a stable North American trading system and an ordered and predictable system.
If the decision is made at a later date to enter into very specific negotiations, I am confident that would be done over a protracted period of time. The recent free trade agreement signed with Israel, for instance, is to be achieved over a 10 year period.
Let me highlight how important our trading relationship is with the United States.

November 5, 1985
Adjournment Debate
From 1960, our exports to the United States accounted for 56 per cent of our total exports. In 1984 that figure had climbed to over 75 per cent. On the import side, 71 per cent of our total imports are from the United States. Exports, as a percentage of our GNP, have grown in a very favourable way from 12 per cent in 1960 to 25.8 per cent now. A full third of what we produce is exported. The export market accounts for two million jobs in the country. Over a 24-year period, some 474,000 manufacturing jobs have been created in Canada. All but a handful of those jobs can be attributed to export trade.
It is a very important topic, one which we need to approach carefully with our counterparts in the United States. Other trade regimes have been organized in the world. It is a different world out there. We must remain competitive. We cannot put our head in the sand and think that things are not happening. For example, the Japanese and the Koreans are very competitive. If we are to get to the Government's main thrust, which is economic renewal in the country, I submit that we need confidence and good judgment to approach the whole subject, in order to get the country moving on a long-term basis and to create much needed jobs.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-SUGAR-BEET INDUSTRY-PLIGHT OF FARMERS. (B) REQUEST FOR STABILIZATION PAYMENT
AGRICULTURE-SUGAR-BEET INDUSTRY-PLIGHT OF FARMERS. (B) REQUEST FOR STABILIZATION PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I put a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) on October 21 concerning the Government's intention regarding the sugar-beet industry in western Canada, especially in southern Alberta, where some 580 sugar-beet producers planted some 12,900 hectares in crop last year. It is a very important industry to southern Alberta. Some 550 jobs have been created in the plant operation at Taber. It is about a $170 million business.
This is the first year in 60 years that a sugar-beet crop was not actually planted in southern Alberta. As I said, it is a very important industry to that part of the country.
The industry creates about $500 million worth of business across the country. Four times since 1976, the Government has made stabilization payments. In 1976, it was $1.3 million; in 1977 it was $1.1 million; in the crop year 1981 it was $5.9 million; and in the crop year 1982, it was $10.2 million.
In a letter written to me several months ago the Minister indicated that he did not think he would be able to provide any stabilization payments. However, he indicated in a later exchange in the House that he did not remember actually sending that letter to me, although I do have a copy of it.
What is important tonight is that the Government commit itself to two things in order to help the sugar beet producers. First, the Government should commit itself to a stabilization payment for the 1983 crop year, a payment which has been estimated to be somewhere between $15 million and $18 million. I undestand that the Minister has stood up the producers five times. There were meetings which he had agreed to attend at which he did not show up and there were meetings that were cancelled at the last minute. The Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) indicated in a meeting that he had with the sugar producers in late July that he would have a long-term sugar policy made available by October. October has come and gone and still no commitment has been made.
If there is going to be a sugar-beet industry not only in southern Alberta but in Manitoba and Quebec, a commitment by the Government to a stabilization payment for the 1983 crop year must be made and the payment should be due and payable now. There is no problem with the retroactivity of the payment. It used to be a legal problem but that was resolved with the passage of the stabilization Bill earlier this year.
It is essential that this payment be made now. As well, it is essential that there be a long-term commitment to a sugar policy. That commitment was promised by the Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board who has been dealing with this problem. It is essential that the Government commit itself to this important industry.
The sugar-beet industry produces some $500 million worth of products used by Canadian consumers. It involves almost 1,000 jobs across the country, it is a vital industry. This is the first year that there has not been a sugar-beet crop planted in some 60 years. I hope that the Government will be able to make a commitment tonight to make the stabilization payment for the 1983 crop year of $15 million to $18 million, depending upon the calculations, as well as making a commitment to a long-term policy that will ensure that the industry continues.
Surely those figures to which I referred earlier regarding stabilization payments from 1976 are relatively small amounts in the scheme of things. That kind of payment is well worth making to save an industry that is important to foreign exchange and to the livelihood of at least 580 sugar-beet

producers in southern Alberta. As well, there are sugar-beet producers in Quebec and Manitoba who will likewise be jeopardized if this stabilization payment is not made and a long-term commitment to a sugar policy is not announced immediately.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have an opportunity to answer the Hon. Member's question. First of all, I can say that I know quite a bit about the situation. At the end of last week, I personally met with sugar beet producers from Southern Alberta here on the Hill, outside the House. I have met with them several times in the course of the year, and 1 even met them in Alberta. The Government has, in fact, already taken a number of steps to help sugar beet producers.
I would like to take this opportunity to clarify the situation raised by the Hon. Member. He felt there were anomalies between the federal Government's treatment of the sugar-beet industry and Ontario tobacco growers. Several points must be taken into consideration in this regard.
In the first place, the Hon. Member is in error when he says that the Minister of Agriculture authorized a $90 million payment to the tobacco industry. No money changed hands. Through the Ontario Flue-cured Tobacco Growers' Marketing Board, the Department provided a loan guarantee so that individual growers could receive cash advances to cover their needs while they store and market their crops the winter months.
The guarantee is handled under the Advance Payments for Crops Act. This Act has been used by a wide range of producer groups since it was passed in 1977. Under this Act there is a $400 million contingency liability which guarantees advances made to producers through their marketing organizations. The marketing organization obtains a loan from a bank or another financial institution and then makes advance payments to its members. The federal Government guarantees the loan and pays the interest charges until the advances are repaid. 1 should mention that there are seldom defaults under this program. Some 99.9 per cent of advances are repaid.
The Tobacco Growers' Marketing Board has applied for this guarantee every year for the past five years. To date, there have been no defaults on advances made to tobacco growers. The sugar growers have never applied for assistance under this program. The sugar growers have requested a stabilization payment, that is, a support payment to compensate for the fact that the bottom has fallen out of the world sugar market and farmers are not receiving adequate returns on their sugar-beet crops.

MARINE TRANSPORT-CONSTRUCTION OF FERRIES. (B) PLACEMENT OF ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity this evening to say something more about the situation in the shipbuilding industry which is of concern to many Canadians. I appreciate this opportunity particularly because I am the only opposition Member with a shipbuilding or ship repair facility in his riding. In my case it is the Port Arthur Shipbuilding Company.
I am concerned about the state of the industry nationally and I am concerned about the industry in my own riding. In my riding there is a great deal of anxiety among the workers of the Port Arthur Shipbuilding Company with respect to the lack of orders the company has received. The management of the company has pointed out to me the difficulties which they face when competition for repair work is so severe because of the relatively few orders coming to the shipbuilding yards across the country, specifically on the Great Lakes.
There is much reason for concern about the shipbuilding policy of the Government. I have had the opportunity to articulate some of those concerns. I must say that as days pass and the Government says nothing, makes no announcements, I become more and more concerned. After all, more than four months ago, on June 27, I asked the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) whether or not he would wait months and months more to provide some answers to the needs of the shipbuilding industry. And he said in one word, "no". But four months have in fact passed and everyone in the industry, and we in the House of Commons, await a statement of policies to follow which would make a real difference.
I am, however, not addressing those general considerations so much as the particular question of the addition of vessels to the fleet of CN Marine in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. I address that particular matter for a couple of reasons; First, because of

the fact that Government Orders are of enormous importance to the industry, given a lack of appropriate policy and, second, because as La Presse has pointed out just in the last day or two, there are in fact fewer vessels under construction in the shipyards these days than there are shipyards in existence. That underscores the fact that when Government does nothing in the way of commercial orders, it becomes imperative that the possibility of public orders. Government contracts of various sorts which now provide some business, remains a possibility.
What we quite specifically have for our focus is a statement by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) which was made almost a year ago. I am going to read that statement because it is quite central to our concern, and I quote from Hansard, page 217:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the Hon. Member's question, it really is a twofold proposition. There will be a rationalization of the Gulf ferry services and the coastal ferry services. As a matter of fact, there will be an additional three new vessels on the Gulf service and one new vessel on the Newfoundland-Labrador coastal service. These vessels will be of the latest state of the art; they will be faster, they will be larger, and they will provide more flexibility and more reliable service. Not only that, this will have a tremendous impact upon the shipbuilding industry and, therefore, will create jobs.
That statement on November 14, 1984, is of enormous importance to people in the industry. When reports surfaced last week that CN Marine might in fact be allowed to import a vessel rather than ordering and having built in Canada a state of the art vessel, I had real reason to raise questions in the House. The Minister's answers were not satisfactory. They were in fact cause for the gravest concern.
In 1979, may I remind you, Mr. Speaker, and Hon. Members of the House, the Conservatives had achieved power and came to office on the basis of many promises, including the promise to build up the shipping industry, to encourage it. It allowed CN Marine very soon thereafter to obtain from Scandinavia two vessels on long-term lease, and by that action prevented the opportunity for construction of these vessels in Canada. At the moment the shipbuilding firm of Versatile Davie in Lauzon, Quebec is near completion of the Caribou. That is one addition to the CN Marine fleet.
The question is will the promise of the Minister of Transport on November 14, 1984, that another such vessel would be built in Canada, be kept? The Minister's statements a week ago today were anything but reassuring. In fact, there was enough cause for concern that one of his colleagues, the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine), presented a report to him on the following day, Wednesday, which pointed out that the cost advantages which CN Marine was putting forward with respect to a vessel from Scandinavia were largely elusory. If one takes a purchase price, of, let us say, $40 million and converts it into U.S. dollars, then puts a duty of 25 per cent on that, then applies the refitting effort which would be required to bring the vessel to scratch, whether it was done outside or within Canada, one would in fact end up with a vessel cost of perhaps $110 million in Canadian dollars. Versatile Davie is completing construction of the Caribou, I am told, at the price of about $117 million. So the difference is very small.
You can appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that the construction of the vessel at Versatile Davie would create 2,000 person years of work so that 50 per cent of that cost is likely to go for wages and an additional very large amount of money to Canadian suppliers of materials and so on. We can see that the impact on the economy of the Quebec City area, and of suppliers beyond that, and the return to Government in the way of income tax and corporation taxes, would be quite sufficient. On the other hand, if the work is not there, we are going to see people on unemployment insurance and the Government will be forced to incur other costs while CN Marine tries to get away with saving a little.
The question is then: Is the Government going to keep its promise? Is the Minister of Transport going to stand by his words of November, 1984? I look forward to a response from the Parliamentary Secretary who I know has the interests of shipbuilding very deep at heart. What will the Government do?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. M. Forrestall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MARINE TRANSPORT-CONSTRUCTION OF FERRIES. (B) PLACEMENT OF ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's comments are appropriate and reflect a genuine concern. I assure him that those concerns are shares by this Government.
The Government is aware of its responsibility to provide good and efficient ferry services at a reasonable, efficient and effective cost. To this end the motor vessel Caribou, constructed at Davie shipbuilding, Lauzon, Quebec, will operate on the North Sydney to Port-aux-Basques ferry service. This vessel, built at a cost of $121 million, has a capacity of 350 automobiles and 1,200 passengers, and is expected to commence service in early 1986. As well, a new passenger-freight vessel is under construction at the Port Weller dry docks in St. Catherines for the Newfoundland and Labrador coastal service. The vessel, built at a cost of $20 million, will have a capacity of 130 passengers and will replace the aging motor vessel Bona-vista which has served now for some 28 years.
Both these projects give work to Canadian workers, using Canadian materials in Canadian shipyards. The motor vessel Caribou was the first phase of the rationalization of the Gulf ferry services undertaken by CN Marine. The new service will consist of the motor vessel Caribou, a roll-on-roll-off vessel which will be assigned to carry containers, and a new passenger vessel for the North Sydney-Argentia service. The latter ship will replace the motor vessel Ambrose Shea and be similar to the Caribou but with additional passenger cabins.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) informed the Hon. Member, in response to his question of October 29, that methods of acquisition of the roll-on-roll-off vessel and the second passenger vessel are under consideration by CN Marine at this time.
In reply to the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine), on a similar question on October 31, the Minister gave his assurance that the report sent to him by this new yet very knowl-
